cards.use_when: Diagnosing which experience metric is hurting a homepage, category page, PDP or checkout, and setting fix priorities.
steps: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) — time until the largest visible element loads, typically the homepage hero or the PDP product image. Target under 2.5 seconds. If it fails, shoppers may doubt the store's credibility or functionality before they even see the product.

CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) — visual stability of elements. Target under 0.1. High CLS causes misclicks when buttons or elements move just before a tap; the source notes the worst case is purchase abandonment from frustration with an unstable interface.

INP (Interaction to Next Paint) — responsiveness to interactions such as clicking 'Add to cart'. INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) in March 2024. Target under 200 milliseconds. Delayed response in checkout makes users click repeatedly or abandon because they are unsure their input registered.
TTFB (Time to First Byte) — server response time from request to first byte. Target under 800 milliseconds, which the source notes is often harder to achieve in ecommerce because of dynamic carts.
Read TTFB as a foundation signal: poor TTFB points to slow hosting or an overloaded database, and frontend work can only do so much if the base is weak.
caveats: Editorial correction: LCP, INP and CLS are the three Core Web Vitals; TTFB is diagnostic. Assess the 75th percentile separately for mobile and desktop. https://web.dev/articles/vitals
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Where ecommerce stores lose speed: five common killers
cards.summary: The recurring causes of slow storefronts — images, third-party scripts, plugins, missing caching, and unused CSS/JS.
cards.use_when: Running a speed audit on a live store to decide which fix class will recover the most seconds.
steps: Unoptimized images: high-resolution product photos are needed for sales, but PNG/JPEG inflate page weight. Modern formats (WebP/AVIF) cut file size 30–50% at the same quality. Images can make up more than 60% of a page's total data volume, making them the biggest lever.

Third-party scripts: tracking pixels, chat widgets, review platforms and social embeds each load their own JavaScript and block rendering. In many stores these external requests account for more than 50% of total load time.
Plugins: every app or plugin loads its own stylesheets and scripts. Especially harmful are plugins that run complex database queries on every page load without caching results.

Missing caching: without it, the server rebuilds each page on every click — querying databases, calculating prices, assembling layouts. Full-page caching instead serves a pre-rendered version, sharply cutting response times.
Site-wide CSS/JS: many themes load functionality on every page even when only one subpage needs it, so mobile browsers download and process unused code.
caveats: The >50% script share and >60% image data share are source-reported typical figures, not fixed proportions in every store; confirm with your own audit.
Do not remove review, chat or tracking scripts purely on speed grounds without checking their revenue or operational role.
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Baseline first: measuring speed before you change anything
cards.summary: Establish a documented before-state with PageSpeed Insights on mobile and desktop so each optimisation can be attributed.
cards.use_when: Starting any speed project on a store, or when you need evidence that a technical change actually helped.
steps: Run Google PageSpeed Insights for your URL on both mobile and desktop before touching anything, since mobile and desktop scores diverge and your mobile traffic is the larger revenue share.
Record the LCP value (and other CWV values) plus the overall score for each template you care about — homepage, key category pages, best-selling PDPs, cart and checkout.
Keep a dated change log in plain text, e.g. 'March 15 – image compression enabled', so you can tie observed metric shifts to specific actions instead of arguing about causes.
Repeat the same measurements after each change class (images, plugins, caching) rather than bundling everything, so you can tell which lever produced which gain and roll back anything that regresses.
Use the before/after numbers as the internal evidence for continuing or stopping further investment in speed work.
caveats: PageSpeed Insights is Google's tool and its interface and scoring can change — verify current reports when you run it.
Lab scores do not equal real-user field data; treat them as directional for prioritisation.
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Optimise product images with WebP/AVIF and responsive sizes
cards.summary: Convert legacy JPEG/PNG to modern formats and serve device-appropriate sizes to cut page weight 30–50%.
cards.use_when: Reducing PDP and category page weight while keeping product photography high-resolution enough to sell.
steps: Convert legacy PNG and JPEG assets to WebP or AVIF, which the source reports reduce file size by 30–50% at the same visual quality — the highest-leverage single fix when images are the bulk of page data.
For a small number of images, convert them manually with free browser-based tools; for a catalogue-scale store, use platform automation instead of hand-editing.
On Shopware 6, rely on automatic WebP generation for uploaded source images and automatic thumbnail sets that produce multiple sizes per product, so each device gets an appropriately sized file.
Keep the original high-resolution source so you can regenerate renditions if your format or size strategy changes.
Re-measure LCP on your hero image (homepage) and main product image (PDP) after conversion, since these are the elements LCP scores.
caveats: Shopware automation details are platform-specific; other carts need equivalent plugins or CDN image services — verify your platform's current capabilities.
Format support and compression results vary by image type; check visual quality on product close-ups before bulk converting.
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Plugin and script audit: earn each extension its place
cards.summary: Review your plugin list against revenue contribution, then disable, measure and delete.
cards.use_when: Cleaning up accumulated plugins, apps and marketing pixels that slow rendering on store pages.
steps: Open your plugin list in the admin panel and review it from top to bottom, asking of each one: 'How does this plugin currently contribute to revenue?'
Flag the usual offenders: marketing pixels, unused design effects, chat widgets and plugins that run uncached database queries on every page load.
Disable uncertain plugins in a staging environment — not on live — then measure page speed again and compare against your baseline.
Remove unused plugins completely rather than merely deactivating them, since leftover code and assets can still be loaded or interfere.
Repeat the loop for third-party scripts: every tracking pixel, review widget, chat tool and social embed adds blocking JavaScript, so only keep those whose measured value justifies their cost.
caveats: Never disable tracking or review scripts on live without confirming you are not breaking attribution, customer service or social proof.
Staging environments may not replicate production traffic or caching, so confirm gains on live after a controlled rollout.
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Server-side foundation: caching, PHP and HTTP/3
cards.summary: The back-end levers — Redis or Varnish full-page caching, PHP 8.2+ and HTTP/3 — that must precede frontend polish.
cards.use_when: Escalating to your host or IT team after content-level fixes, when TTFB or overall response time is still poor.
steps: Finish content and plugin work first: the source explicitly advises contacting your provider only after steps 1–3, otherwise support will simply point at your unoptimized images and scripts.

Ask specifically whether server-side caching such as Redis or Varnish is active, and whether full-page caching delivers pre-rendered HTML instead of rebuilding pages (querying databases and recalculating prices) on every click.
Ask for the current PHP version and whether your stack is on PHP 8.2+ and HTTP/3; these are the modern server technologies the source recommends as the foundation for all further optimisation.
In SaaS or cloud environments, many settings may already be optimised — still review the documentation and confirm rather than assume.
After infrastructure changes, re-run your baseline measurements for TTFB and LCP to verify the server improvement reached the storefront.
caveats: These stack recommendations reflect the source's guidance and will age; verify current supported PHP and HTTP versions before requesting changes.
Infrastructure changes can interact badly with checkout and cart logic — test transactional flows after any caching or protocol change.
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Platform-native caching and intelligent cache invalidation
cards.summary: Using built-in full-page cache, automatic WebP, thumbnail sets and selective invalidation instead of manual workarounds.
cards.use_when: Choosing or configuring an ecommerce platform's performance features, especially where price and stock updates must not serve stale pages.
steps: Use the platform's integrated HTTP cache so repeat visits are served pre-rendered HTML rather than re-executing PHP and querying the database.
Rely on native WebP generation for uploaded images and automatic thumbnail sets so each device receives an appropriately sized file without a custom pipeline.

Understand intelligent cache invalidation: the platform detects price or stock changes and clears only the affected pages rather than purging the entire site cache — keeping the store fast without displaying outdated prices or availability.
Confirm your platform also bundles and optimises required CSS and JavaScript, avoiding site-wide loading of code needed on only one subpage.
Where your platform lacks these features, look for equivalent automatic image conversion, responsive thumbnail generation and selective cache purging before building custom tooling.
caveats: Shopware 6 is the source's example of a platform with these native features; other platforms differ, so verify current capabilities in your own admin and documentation.
Selective invalidation depends on correct price/stock event wiring — test that price and availability changes actually propagate before trusting the cache.
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Prioritised speed roadmap for a store
cards.summary: A sequenced order of work — baseline, images, extensions, then infrastructure — so each fix can be measured and credited.
cards.use_when: Planning a multi-week speed programme and deciding what to do first with limited developer or agency time.
steps: Step 1 — Baseline: run PageSpeed Insights for mobile and desktop, log LCP and the overall score, and start a dated change log.
Step 2 — Images: convert to WebP/AVIF and serve responsive sizes, since images are typically the largest share of page data and the cheapest early win.
Step 3 — Extensions: review plugins top to bottom against revenue contribution, disable candidates in staging, measure, then delete unused ones completely and trim non-essential third-party scripts.
Step 4 — Infrastructure: with content and scripts cleaned up, ask your host or IT about PHP version and Redis/Varnish server-side caching, and confirm PHP 8.2+ / HTTP/3.
Throughout: use full-page caching with intelligent invalidation so price and stock changes clear only the affected pages, and re-measure after each stage so gains are attributable.
caveats: The sequence is the source's recommended order, not a universal law — a severely underpowered server may justify infrastructure work earlier, but expect reduced credibility with support if content is still unoptimised.
Each stage should be re-measured; bundling all changes makes it impossible to know which one helped.
cards.source_name: Page speed guide for ecommerce store operators_ diagnosis and actions.docx

cards.title: Remove residual Shopify app code from theme files
cards.summary: Uninstalling a Shopify app often leaves injected scripts behind that still fire external requests, so manually search and delete leftover tags in theme.liquid, head.liquid and footer.liquid.
cards.use_when: Auditing loading performance on a Shopify store after installing, trialing or uninstalling speed or marketing apps, before concluding the theme itself is slow.
steps: Inventory apps you have installed or trialed, noting each app's brand name (for example 'loox') because leftover snippets usually contain the app name or its CDN domain.

Search theme files for those names: theme.liquid, head.liquid and footer.liquid are the paths to check. A Chrome extension such as Shopify Theme File Search lets you grep across the theme instead of opening files one by one.
Delete the lingering <script> tags you find. Uninstalling an app does not always remove its injected code, and any surviving tag keeps making requests to an external server on every page load.
Re-test the storefront after each removal so you can attribute any change in load behavior to a specific deletion rather than a batch edit.
Repeat this cleanup periodically, especially after trial installs, since each app adds independent risk of residual code.
caveats: Only remove snippets tied to apps you have actually uninstalled; deleting code for an active app breaks its function.
Keep a backup or version record of theme files before editing Liquid directly.

cards.title: Format and size images and videos for faster load
cards.summary: Cap image files under 1MB, prefer JPEG over PNG unless transparency is needed, and replace heavy animated GIFs with compressed MP4 video in an HTML video tag.
cards.use_when: Merchandising product images, hero banners or category tiles on a Shopify store, or diagnosing pages that load slowly because of large media assets.
steps: Keep image file sizes under 1MB as the working ceiling for storefront assets.
Choose JPEG instead of PNG unless the image genuinely requires transparency; PNG files are usually much heavier for photographic content.
Replace heavy animated GIFs with compressed MP4 video embedded via an HTML <video> tag, which delivers the same motion at far smaller file size.
Apply video loading behavior deliberately: set preload="none" on videos so the browser does not eagerly fetch media the shopper has not reached yet.
Apply loading="lazy" to off-screen images so they are only fetched as the shopper scrolls toward them.
Do not lazy load above-the-fold assets such as the hero image; those should load immediately to keep LCP low.
caveats: Lazy loading the hero image works against LCP rather than helping it.
Transparency requirements and animation content determine whether the JPEG or GIF-replacement advice applies to a given asset.

cards.title: Lazy load below-fold media, preload the hero
cards.summary: Use loading=lazy for off-screen images and preload=none for video, but preload above-the-fold assets with a link in the head instead of lazy loading them.
cards.use_when: Structuring a product page, landing page or homepage where the hero image and other above-the-fold media compete with below-fold content for bandwidth.
steps: Identify the assets visible in the initial viewport, typically the hero image and any headline banner. These are the ones that determine LCP.
For above-the-fold assets, do not apply loading="lazy". Instead add a preload link in the <head> so the browser fetches them at the earliest opportunity.
For every image below the fold, add loading="lazy" so the request is deferred until the shopper scrolls near it.
For embedded videos, set preload="none" to prevent the browser from downloading video data on page load.
Re-check after restructuring that the hero still renders promptly and that below-fold content does not appear late or jumpy.
caveats: Applying lazy loading indiscriminately to all images including the hero is the common failure mode this addresses.
Which asset counts as above-the-fold changes by viewport size, so check mobile and desktop layouts separately.

cards.title: Reduce storefront script blocking while preserving purchase tracking
cards.summary: Audit script loading without breaking product interactions or analytics events.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing render-blocking scripts on a Shopify storefront, or speeding up page rendering without breaking analytics and ad tracking during acquisition campaigns.
steps: Inventory theme and app scripts; remove confirmed unused integrations on a duplicate theme first.
Choose defer or async only after checking execution order, DOM dependencies and the vendor integration requirements.
Do not impose a blanket synchronous-pixel rule. Use the supported platform integration; Shopify provides a Web Pixels API and standard event subscriptions.
Test consent behavior, page views, variant selection, add-to-cart and a test purchase after changes; check missing and duplicate events.
caveats: Editorial correction: source advice that all pixels must remain synchronous is not a universal requirement. Verify the specific integration. https://shopify.dev/docs/api/pixels

cards.title: Load non-critical CSS asynchronously with the media=print trick
cards.summary: Use media="print" onload="this.media='all'" on non-critical stylesheets so they download without blocking the rendering path.
cards.use_when: Cutting render-blocking CSS on product, category or landing pages where multiple stylesheets delay first paint.
steps: Identify stylesheets that are not required for the initial render, such as styles for modals, below-fold sections or secondary components.

Rewrite those link tags as <link rel="stylesheet" href="..." media="print" onload="this.media='all'">. The browser treats the print stylesheet as non-render-blocking and downloads it without stalling paint.
Leave critical above-the-fold CSS loaded normally, since it is needed for first render.
Apply the same async pattern to any additional non-critical stylesheets you introduce later.
Test the page visually after the change to confirm the deferral did not cause a flash of unstyled content in areas the shopper sees immediately.
caveats: Moving critical CSS into this pattern can leave the visible page unstyled on first paint.
This is a specific HTML attribute technique; verify the markup still behaves as expected in the current browser and theme context.

cards.title: Set font-display: swap to prevent invisible text
cards.summary: Add font-display: swap to every @font-face declaration so text renders in a system font immediately instead of staying blank while the custom font downloads.
cards.use_when: Fixing slow text rendering, low perceived speed or a flash of invisible text on product pages that use custom brand fonts.
steps: Open the stylesheet containing the store's @font-face declarations.
Add font-display: swap to each @font-face rule. This tells the browser to render text in a fallback system font immediately and swap in the custom font once it loads.
Without swap, the browser can leave text blank until the custom font finishes downloading, which reads as a broken or slow page to the shopper.
Confirm the change covers all custom font declarations, including weights and italic variants loaded separately.
Review the page after the change to ensure the swap does not introduce disruptive layout shift when the brand font replaces the fallback.
caveats: Swap improves perceived speed but can cause a visible font switch; check that fallback and brand fonts have similar metrics to limit reflow.
Custom font files should still be reasonably sized; font-display only changes how the wait is presented.

cards.title: Approach speed work as rendering mechanics, not app shortcuts
cards.summary: Prioritize deferring scripts, cleaning residual theme code, formatting media and using CSS media attributes to unblock the main rendering thread instead of relying on superficial speed apps.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate effort on a Shopify speed problem, choosing between installing a speed app and editing theme code, or setting a performance baseline for the storefront.
steps: Treat loading performance, browser rendering, perceived performance, resource optimization, Core Web Vitals, caching and file-size reduction as the core problem set.
Work on the actual mechanisms: defer non-essential scripts, remove leftover app code from Liquid templates, size and format media correctly, and use CSS media attributes to load non-critical styles.

Be skeptical of approaches aimed mainly at spoofing Lighthouse scores rather than improving real rendering and load behavior, and of general complaints about pushy apps or speed specialists that do not identify a concrete fix.
Keep paid social creative formats and true incremental ROAS or pixel/CAPI setups in their own workstreams, since they are separate from loading performance.
Establish a baseline measurement before editing so speed changes can be judged against it.
caveats: The source's framing of speed work as theme-level mechanics is a stance; some stores may still need managed hosting or app-level solutions.
Perceived-performance changes are not always captured by a single synthetic score.

cards.title: Shopify image pipeline audit: what Shopify does and doesn't optimize
cards.summary: Shopify auto-converts uploads to WebP and serves them via CDN with theme-controlled widths, but leaves resize compression, wrong-format images and unoptimized theme sections to you.
cards.use_when: Auditing product images or theme assets for page speed on a Shopify store
steps: Recognize the free wins already in place: Shopify serves images from a CDN (copies propagate to regional servers, so distant customers download locally) and lazily generates width variants from one upload via URL filters such as appending ?width=493, so the theme can request a smaller rendition instead of the master file.

Verified behavior on a test store: a 9.8 MB upload was auto-reduced to roughly 6.1 MB on delivery, but the presenter recommends 500 KB as the practical ceiling — meaning out-of-the-box compression is real but conservative. Do not assume upload equals optimized.

Shopify also serves WebP automatically to browsers that support it (a JPEG upload downloads as .webp). Do not pre-convert your catalog to WebP: if you serve only WebP and a browser doesn't support it, shoppers see no image. Upload JPEG/PNG and let Shopify handle format negotiation.

Find the gaps: (1) large dimensions are not reduced enough, (2) the wrong source format (PNG/GIF where JPEG would do) cannot be repaired by Shopify, (3) whether a theme requests multiple widths is determined by the theme code, not Shopify.
Prioritize images because they are among the heaviest assets and the part you can actually control, unlike apps and platform code.
caveats: Shopify's internal dashboards and CDN behavior change over time — verify current upload sizes and filter parameters in the live admin before building a process around specifics.
The 500-600 KB ceiling and the 6.1 MB observation are this presenter's test values, not Shopify-published benchmarks.

cards.title: Check whether your theme serves responsive image widths
cards.summary: Inspect theme Liquid to see whether image tags emit multiple width sources or push the full master image to every device.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing slow mobile PDP or homepage load on a custom, agency-built or older Shopify theme
steps: Open Online Store → Themes → Edit code and open a section or snippet that renders an image (hero, image-with-text, product grid).

A bad pattern looks like a single img src pointing at image.url or image | img_url: 'master'. That means every device — phone and 4K desktop alike — downloads the identical original file, so a 5,000px upload is delivered to a 400px screen.

The desired pattern is a srcset (or equivalent srcset-style Liquid filter) offering several widths, e.g. a 1,600px default plus entries for 800px and 1,200px, so the browser fetches the smallest adequate file.

If your theme is old, custom or agency-modified, audit all image-bearing sections rather than one: sections added later by developers often skip the responsive pattern even when the base theme uses it.
Fix or have fixed the offending sections; the presenter calls this the first thing to check on a store, because the payoff is immediate and applies to all traffic, especially mobile.
caveats: Newer Shopify themes generally follow this practice; old or heavily customized themes are the usual offenders.
Verifying responsive behavior requires reading theme code or inspecting network requests per viewport, which many merchants cannot do alone.

cards.title: Choose JPEG, PNG, WebP or MP4 by image role
cards.summary: Match source format to whether the image needs transparency, photographic detail or animation.
cards.use_when: Preparing product photos, banners, logos or animated promos before upload
steps: Default for photography and any rectangular image without transparency: JPEG. It supports lossy compression, which the human eye largely cannot detect at sensible settings, and Shopify converts it to WebP.

Use PNG only when you need transparency or crisp flat graphics: cut-out product shots that must sit on a colored section, logos, and illustrations layered over other content. In the example store, a transparent cut-out product and a transparent logo justified PNG; the same product on a white background could have been a better-compressing JPEG.
Avoid PNG for ordinary opaque photos. Demonstrated cost: the identical image re-exported as PNG with no edits went from 2.7 MB to 8 MB purely from the format.
Avoid GIF for animation. Use MP4 video in an HTML video tag instead — it loads far better than an animated GIF.

Lossless (PNG) preserves quality for further editing; lossy (JPEG) discards detail you mostly cannot see and is the format for delivery. You can still compress PNGs, so an oversized PNG is never necessary.
caveats: Do not convert and upload WebP yourself; Shopify's automatic conversion is what keeps non-supporting browsers served.
Format advice assumes normal ecommerce viewing; print or archival use has different requirements.

cards.title: Size and compress product images before upload
cards.summary: Cap dimensions around 2,000px on the long edge and file size around 100-500 KB, with compression judged visually rather than by number alone.
cards.use_when: Preparing a photo shoot or supplier image drop for a product launch or catalog refresh
steps: Resize the long edge. The presenter's rule: never upload larger than 3,000px, and 3,000 is already overkill — 2,000px is enough for hero banners, zoom and retina on typical Full HD and 4K screens. Because screens downscale, an 8,000px image and a 2,000px image look effectively the same on a 3,000px-wide display.

Size to the box, not the screen. A 600x600 grid tile should receive roughly a 600px-class image; feeding it 5,000px wastes bandwidth (a ~3 MB asset where ~60 KB would do). Only full-bleed elements like a hero justify near screen width.

Compress with a visual preview. A tool with a live preview (the presenter uses Squoosh) lets you drag the quality slider and stop when artifacts appear: at quality 40 a 2.7 MB image landed at 172 KB with no difference the presenter could see, and quality 20-30 remained acceptable in his view.
Ceiling guidance: stay under 500-600 KB, and preferably 100-200 KB. A real reference point from an example store: a 1,920x1,920 zoomable product image at 46 KB looked fine.

Do image resizing and format conversion before upload. Shopify's built-in editor can resize and change aspect ratio, but offers no compression settings — so an oversized upload stays oversized in weight.
caveats: Numbers are the presenter's working thresholds, not a universal standard; heavily textured images may need higher quality settings to avoid visible artifacts.
Fine line art, small text in images and print use tolerate compression far less well.

cards.title: Batch resize in Preview, crop individually, then convert format
cards.summary: Resizing can be automated across a folder; cropping and format export must be checked per image.
cards.use_when: Processing a folder of photographer or supplier images before loading them into Shopify
steps: Keep a folder of same-orientation images, select them all, open in macOS Preview, then Edit → Select All and Tools → Adjust Size. Set the larger dimension (e.g. 4,000) down to 2,000 and apply — this resizes the whole batch in one pass.

Do not batch crop. Product framing differs image to image, so a shared crop rectangle decapitates some products. Crop manually instead: in Preview use the selection tool, hold Shift to constrain to a square, position it, then click the crop icon.
Export to JPEG or PNG: File → Export lets you change the format (e.g. iPhone HEIC to JPEG) and apply compression in one step, with a file-size readout.

Understand the limitation of that export dialog: it shows resulting file size but not image quality, so you are accepting the setting blind. For control, do the compression step in a preview-based tool where you can see the result.
This sequence (resize → crop → convert → compress → rename → alt text → upload) is the recommended order; doing it in another order creates rework.
caveats: Bulk resizing assumes uniform orientation; mixing portrait and landscape in one batch will resize the wrong axis.
Windows equivalents exist but the presenter only demonstrates the macOS Preview workflow.

cards.title: Automate image compression for large catalogs
cards.summary: Use a bulk optimization app when manual per-image compression is impractical, and let it compress on upload.
cards.use_when: Running a store with a large or already-loaded image catalog that needs compressing at scale
steps: Estimate the workload first: manual per-image compression with a preview tool works for a handful of hero or launch images, but for a large catalog — especially images already uploaded to Shopify — it is a lot of repetitive manual work.

Install an image optimization app (the presenter uses Tiny SEO Speed and Image Optimizer) and enable automatic compression of images as they upload, so compression stops being a step you remember to do.
Check the app's optimization report for per-image savings from actual runs. In the presenter's example, individual images lost more than 80% of their file size after optimization.
Treat size reduction as a bandwidth and experience win for the shopper, not only a Lighthouse number.
Keep the manual pipeline for launch hero images and for anything the app compresses too aggressively, since you control quality only in a preview tool.
caveats: Installing an app adds its own scripts and can offset speed gains from compression — measure before and after.
App results and features vary; verify current app capabilities in the Shopify App Store, as interfaces change.
Some apps also alter SEO fields; review their settings rather than accepting defaults.

cards.title: Fix messy product grids with Shopify's crop and resize tools
cards.summary: Crop uploaded images to your theme's aspect ratio inside Shopify so the collection grid stays visually consistent.
cards.use_when: Product grid or collection page looks uneven because uploaded images have mixed aspect ratios
steps: Establish the grid's aspect ratio first. Commonly used online: square for general product grids, and 4:5 portrait for fashion, which fits a full-body model shot better.

Fix already-uploaded images without re-uploading: open the image in the Shopify media editor, use crop and transform to pick the target ratio (square is offered as a preset), drag the crop frame to keep the whole product in view, then Apply.
Resize dimensions in the same editor if the file is oversized; the presenter changed 3,000 to 1,920 for a square product image as a sufficient size for zoom.
Save, then refresh the collection page to confirm the grid is aligned.
Prevent the problem upstream: crop to the target ratio before upload, since a tall image added to a square grid renders visibly out of step with its neighbors.
caveats: Shopify's in-admin editor resizes and crops but offers no compression settings, so its output can remain heavier than a properly compressed pre-upload file.
Changing the main image's crop changes how the product appears in collection grids; check the storefront, not just the admin preview.

cards.title: Plan a product image set: 3-5 images that each answer a question
cards.summary: Shoot main, alternate angle, detail and lifestyle shots, adding more only for higher-priced or complex products.
cards.use_when: Planning a product photo shoot or deciding which images to add to a PDP
steps: Start with the minimum that answers buying questions: three to five images. One is workable, two is better, three to five covers most stores.

Cover the four functional slots: a main hero shot, an alternate angle (side, back or top depending on the product), a detail shot showing a feature, and a lifestyle shot of the product in use or held.

Add more depth for higher-priced or more complex products, where extra angles, kit contents and multiple usage scenarios help the shopper imagine owning the item and justify the price. Reference examples show footwear/apparel and sporting goods running the four-slot pattern, plus video.

Test a reordered gallery when the product is aspirational: the presenter suggests main image, alternate angle, lifestyle, then details, so the shopper imagines ownership first and resolves objections second.
Stop adding when no image is answering a new question — filler images add page weight and make mobile scrolling excessive.
caveats: The 3-5 figure is a practical heuristic, not a measured conversion threshold.
Extra images are only affordable if they are correctly sized and lazy-loaded, otherwise they degrade mobile performance.

cards.title: Name image files with keyword-first descriptive filenames
cards.summary: Use a repeating filename formula — main keyword, product descriptor, unique detail, angle — instead of camera or supplier filenames.
cards.use_when: Renaming a folder of product images before uploading them to Shopify
steps: Reject camera/supplier filenames (random strings, IMG_1234) — they give search engines nothing to categorize the image with, so you lose an SEO opportunity at upload time. For images already uploaded with bad names, replacing the file is the practical remedy.
Use the formula: main keyword + product descriptor + unique detail + shot angle. Examples from the source: leather-wallet-men-brown-back, leather-wallet-men-stitched-detail.

Generate these at scale by prompting ChatGPT with a template: supply the main keyword (sports backpack), the descriptor (men), and a comma-separated list of per-image details (black front, top detail, on the shoulder, back, front detail), and take the resulting filenames.
Review the output — in the demonstration the model produced more filenames than images existed, so match names to files deliberately rather than pasting blindly.
Do this before upload, alongside resizing and compression, so each file goes up once, correctly named.
caveats: Filename is a categorization signal only; it is never shown to shoppers. Alt text carries the user-facing and semantic description.
AI-generated names still need human review for accuracy of color, angle and product detail.

cards.title: Write alt text that describes the image, not a sales pitch
cards.summary: Alt text serves accessibility, broken-image fallback and Google's understanding of the image — write natural descriptions and keep ads out.
cards.use_when: Adding or auditing alt text across product images, collection banners and blog images
steps: Write a plain description of what is in the frame, as a sighted shopper would describe it: 'men wearing a black sports backpack outdoors' or 'closeup of padded shoulder straps on a black sports backpack'.
Use the filename for initial categorization and alt text for meaning — Google uses both, and alt text is also the text that displays when an image fails to load, so the page still communicates.
Accessibility is a real functional reason, not a checkbox: visually impaired shoppers navigate the store through this text, and missing alt text shuts them out.

Avoid promotional copy in alt text ('leather wallet man black buy cheap'). The presenter's position is that this is poor practice — though still better than no alt text at all, since the image at least stays indexed.
Do it for every shot in the gallery, matching each alt text to that specific angle or detail rather than repeating the product name.
caveats: The source treats ad-laden alt text as a mistake but explicitly ranks it above blank alt text; the trade-off is indexation versus quality.
Alt text must not be used to stuff keywords — the examples are natural sentences.

cards.title: Upload product images and assign variant images so color swatches switch the gallery
cards.summary: Understand that all uploads land in the shared media library, and attach the right image to each variant.
cards.use_when: Building a new product page or adding a new color variant with its own photography
steps: Know the entry points: images can be uploaded from Content → Files (the media library), directly on the product creation page (upload new or select existing), on collection pages for cover images, on blog posts, and through the theme customizer for section images. Everything lands in the same media library.
On the product page, drag to set the order: main image first, then alternate angle, then lifestyle and details (or details before lifestyle if you prefer question-answering order). Save.

For variants, assign per-option images. In the product editor, each variant row has a plus icon; click it to attach the matching image (e.g. the red backpack for the red variant). After saving, the variant icon shows the assigned thumbnail.
Add new variant photography by uploading through the same plus flow, then click Done and Save so the swatch updates.
Confirm on the storefront: clicking color swatches should swap the gallery image, and variant images should also appear further down the product page.
caveats: Assign every variant a real image — an unassigned variant shows the generic placeholder and can confuse shoppers choosing a color.
Gallery order and variant behavior are theme-dependent; verify in the live theme, not just the admin.

cards.title: Reuse one media-library file per image and use Replace to update everywhere
cards.summary: Duplicated uploads create gibberish URLs, break bulk updates and require you to find every copy when an image changes.
cards.use_when: Maintaining a media library where product, collection, blog and theme images overlap
steps: Upload a given image once and select it from the media library wherever it is needed — product page, collection cover, blog, theme section — rather than uploading the file again.
Understand the consequence of duplicates: uploading the same filename twice produces a second file with a modified, gibberish-suffixed URL. SEO suffers, and future edits multiply.

Use Replace image in the media library when the asset changes. The URL is preserved and only the file is swapped, so every place the image appears — product pages, sections, collections — updates at once. This is the payoff for not having duplicates.
With duplicates, this efficiency disappears: you must locate every copy and replace each individually.
If your media library already has duplicates, consolidate to a single canonical file before a major image refresh.
caveats: Replacing a file changes every usage, including hero images where the new crop may not fit — check each placement after replacing.
Reusing one file across product and banner contexts may force one crop to serve two different aspect ratios.

cards.title: Diagnose whether images are a plausible cause of your speed problem
cards.summary: Use store characteristics — theme age, customization, catalog size, mobile traffic share, app load — to decide if image work is your highest-leverage fix.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to start on a Shopify speed project or whether to invest in image cleanup
steps: If you run an older theme that doesn't receive updates, check images: old themes often don't follow current responsive-width practice, so a single large asset may be served to every device.

If your theme was built or heavily modified by an agency or developer, audit the image tags in its sections — quality varies by builder. Large catalogs with many images per product compound the problem.
If a large share of traffic is mobile, treat images as high priority: mobile devices neither need nor handle large assets well, and unstable connections make heavy downloads worse.
If your store is simple with few apps and still slow, images are a likely culprit and an easy win — compress and re-upload and you may be done.
The presenter's broader point: apps and some platform issues are outside your control, but image weight is controllable, so it is worth doing even when other causes exist.
caveats: The presenter works from experience, not a measurement methodology. Confirm with your own performance data before attributing slowness to images.
Image work is easy but not a substitute for addressing other bottlenecks if images are already optimized.

cards.title: Lazy-load images so catalog size doesn't dictate load weight
cards.summary: Many images are fine if below-the-fold images load only on scroll or interaction — the count matters less than delivery timing.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a media-heavy page or long PDP can carry more images without slowing the load
steps: Reject the assumption that more images means a slower site. The presenter's position: image count is not the problem, as long as the correct sizes are served and images below the fold are lazy-loaded.

Implement lazy loading so an image is fetched only when a trigger fires — a scroll into view, or a defined interaction such as a click. Demonstrated: scrolling populated images that were not downloaded on initial page load, and a click loaded a specific image on demand.
Apply it across long pages: content-heavy pages, long PDP galleries and landing pages with many sections can hold many images without the shopper downloading everything upfront.
Pair lazy loading with correct dimensions. Lazy loading defers weight; it does not shrink oversized files, so both steps are needed.
caveats: Lazy loading above-the-fold hero and LCP images can hurt perceived load — keep those eager.
Theme implementation varies; verify in the live theme, not only in the customizer, and check current best practice before changing loading attributes.

cards.title: Reduce storefront script blocking while preserving purchase tracking
cards.summary: Audit script loading without breaking product interactions or analytics events.
cards.use_when: Reducing JavaScript render blocking in a Shopify theme's liquid files
steps: Inventory theme and app scripts; remove confirmed unused integrations on a duplicate theme first.
Choose defer or async only after checking execution order, DOM dependencies and the vendor integration requirements.
Do not impose a blanket synchronous-pixel rule. Use the supported platform integration; Shopify provides a Web Pixels API and standard event subscriptions.
Test consent behavior, page views, variant selection, add-to-cart and a test purchase after changes; check missing and duplicate events.
caveats: Editorial correction: source advice that all pixels must remain synchronous is not a universal requirement. Verify the specific integration. https://shopify.dev/docs/api/pixels

cards.title: Load non-critical CSS asynchronously
cards.summary: Use the media=print onload swap trick to fetch non-critical stylesheets without blocking render, while keeping critical CSS blocking.
cards.use_when: Reducing render-blocking CSS on a Shopify theme
steps: Identify non-critical stylesheets — anything not needed for the initially visible above-the-fold content.

Load them with the pattern link rel=stylesheet href=... media=print onload="this.media='all'". It downloads the stylesheet in the print media context, which doesn't block rendering, then swaps it to all media once loaded.
Keep the CSS that styles above-the-fold content in a normal blocking stylesheet so the first paint is correct.
Verify the swap actually happens by checking the rendered page and the network panel; a failed onload leaves the stylesheet applied only to print.
Apply the same critical/non-critical split when auditing app-injected CSS, which frequently loads render-blocking assets in the head.
caveats: This is a known hack, not a standard API; behavior depends on browser support for the onload attribute on link elements.
If the swap fails, above-the-fold styling can break, so test across browsers after implementing.

cards.title: Prevent invisible-text flash with font-display: swap
cards.summary: Add font-display: swap inside the @font-face rule so text renders in a fallback immediately while the custom font downloads.
cards.use_when: Custom web fonts on a Shopify theme cause text to be invisible during load
steps: Open the theme stylesheet where custom fonts are declared and locate the @font-face rule.
Add font-display: swap inside that rule. This tells the browser to render text with a system fallback first and swap in the custom font when it arrives, eliminating the flash of invisible text.

Note the trade-off inherent in swap: users may briefly see the fallback font and then a reflow when the custom font loads. The presenter treats this as preferable to invisible text, which delays content for every visitor.
Check other font rules too — a theme may declare several faces, and one missing swap reintroduces the problem for that weight or style.
Test on a slow connection to confirm text is visible during font load.
caveats: Swap produces a visible font change on load; preloading the font is an alternative if you want to shorten the fallback window.
Theme font implementation differs — verify where the @font-face rules live in your specific theme.

cards.title: Replace animated GIFs with MP4 video in a video tag
cards.summary: Animated GIFs are extremely heavy; an MP4 inside an HTML video tag delivers the same motion at far lower weight.
cards.use_when: A product page, homepage section or ad creative uses an animated GIF for motion
steps: Identify the animated GIFs on your store — hero banners, how-it-works sections and product demos are common places.
Convert the animation to MP4 and embed it in an HTML video tag. The presenter states this 'will load much better than a GIF file would', which is why GIF was left out of his recommended format list.
When auditing theme files (theme.liquid, head.liquid, footer.liquid are the paths the presenter checks), look for GIF references that should become video tags.
Keep the same presentation intent — convert first, then verify the section still looks right, since video tags need appropriate sizing and autoplay/mute settings to replace a GIF's visual behavior.
caveats: The source states the speed advantage of MP4 but gives no measured comparison values; treat it as directional.
Video embedding needs correct player attributes (mute, loop, playsinline) to mimic GIF behavior, which the source does not detail.

cards.title: Write descriptive alt text that serves accessibility and image SEO
cards.summary: How to write and apply natural-language alt text to product images so visually impaired shoppers and search engines can understand them.
cards.use_when: You are finalizing product or lifestyle images on a PDP, collection page or homepage and need to set alt text.
steps: Write alt text that describes exactly what is in the image in natural language, as a screen-reader user would need it: 'Men wearing a black sports backpack outdoors.'
Include the product category plus visible attributes and the view/angle: 'Closeup of padded shoulder straps on a black sports backpack' or 'Side view of black sports backpack.'
Avoid stuffing the field with ad copy or keyword strings like 'leather wallet man black buy cheap' — the source says this is the wrong way, though still better than an empty alt field.
To scale across many images, draft a prompt for an AI tool that takes product name, visible characteristics and a list of angles, then generate one alt text per angle.
Paste each result into the image's alt text field (in Shopify, open the image in the editor's alt text field, or edit from Content and Files / media library) and save.
Verify in the live page source that the alt attribute is attached to the image element.
Applying alt text to every image is optional best practice per the source, not a speed factor — prioritize it when accessibility and image search matter for your catalog.
caveats: The source frames this as important for visually impaired users and for Google indexing, not as a page-speed win.
AI-generated alt text must be checked against the actual image; inaccurate descriptions mislead screen-reader users.

cards.title: Match alt text to image angle for multi-image product galleries
cards.summary: Generate distinct alt text for each angle in a product gallery rather than repeating one description.
cards.use_when: You have several images per product (front, back, detail, lifestyle) and are populating alt fields for a PDP gallery.
steps: List the angles you actually shoot for the product — for a backpack: front view, back view, front detail, top detail, lifestyle on shoulder.
Supply product name, visible characteristics (color, water resistance) and that angle list to your AI alt-text prompt so each output maps to one image.
Work through the gallery image by image, pasting the matching alt text into each image and saving.
Use the same angle-first approach when reordering gallery images so the main image, alternate angle, detail shots and lifestyle shots each carry a suitably descriptive alt string.
Re-open the live PDP and inspect each image element to confirm every image has its own alt text rather than a duplicated default.
caveats: The source's angle list is an example for one backpack, not a fixed gallery structure; derive angles from what your own images show.
Some platforms auto-fill alt text from the filename, so verify overrides actually saved.

cards.title: Resize images to just above their display box
cards.summary: Fix oversized images by resizing them to roughly the box they render in plus 100–300px, not the source file's original dimensions.
cards.use_when: You inspect a PDP, hero banner or content section and find the image's intrinsic size far exceeds the size it is displayed at.
steps: Right-click the image in the browser and choose Inspect to read its rendered/intrinsic dimensions against the box it occupies.
Note the display box width — e.g. a section image shown in a 700px box.
Set the new width to the box size plus 100–300px (e.g. ~1,000px for a 700px box) so the image is neither blurry nor oversized.
In the theme customizer, open the section holding the image, click Edit on the uploaded asset, use the native editor's resize function, enter the new width and apply.
Refresh the page and visually confirm the image looks the same as before.
Use the same logic for hero banners: an image 5,712px wide shown in a site capped around 2,000–3,000px can be resized down with no visible change.
Target no more than a few hundred KB per image where possible — resizing alone may still leave a 1MB file that needs compression.
caveats: The native Shopify resize tool reduces dimensions but gives no compression control, so compressing with a separate tool afterward is still required.
The 100–300px overshoot is the source's rule of thumb to avoid blur, not a tested universal threshold.

cards.title: Compress images to keep files small, especially for mobile shoppers
cards.summary: Reduce file weight via compression because resizing alone often leaves files too heavy for mobile connections.
cards.use_when: Your product, banner or section images are still heavy after resizing, and you want faster downloads for mobile visitors.
steps: Audit image file weights in your media library or via page inspection; the source's practical threshold is to reduce any image larger than 500KB.
Resize first if dimensions are oversized, then run the file through a compression tool — the source names Tiny SEO and Squash as examples.
Re-upload the compressed version and confirm the visual result still looks acceptable on the live page.
Check that the new file size dropped materially — the source's example went from ~1MB after resize to roughly 100KB when compressed.
Treat image compression as user-experience work that can also support conversion rate, per the source, rather than only a technical chore.
caveats: Compressing too aggressively can visibly degrade image quality; the source does not specify a quality setting.
The source presents conversion-rate improvement as a possibility tied to better UX, not a measured benchmark.
Compression tools and their interfaces change — verify current options before relying on named tools.

cards.title: Pick the right image format and swap GIFs for MP4
cards.summary: Use JPEG/PNG for still images and MP4 for animation because they load faster.
cards.use_when: You are preparing product, banner or content imagery for upload to a storefront.
steps: Upload stills as JPEG or PNG and let the platform (the source cites Shopify) handle conversion to modern formats like WebP.
Replace animated GIFs with MP4 video, which the source says are better and load faster.
Confirm what your platform auto-converts before doing extra format work yourself, since this reduces the value of manual conversion.
Pair format choice with resizing and compression rather than treating format alone as the fix — the source warns that bad results follow if you upload without resizing or cropping.
caveats: The source's WebP auto-conversion claim is a Shopify behavior that may not apply to other platforms; verify your own pipeline.
Format choice will not rescue files that are still huge in dimension or weight.

cards.title: Name image files descriptively before upload
cards.summary: Give each image a meaningful filename so search engines can categorize it correctly.
cards.use_when: You are about to upload product or content images to your store and are naming the files on your computer.
steps: Rename files to describe what is in the image instead of keeping camera-generated or random names.
Include the product/category and distinguishing attributes (e.g. color or view) so the filename communicates content.
Upload only after renaming, since post-upload filename changes may not carry through cleanly.
Pair descriptive filenames with descriptive alt text — the source lists naming, uploading, reordering, alt text and on-site verification as sequential steps.
caveats: The source treats this as a straightforward SEO benefit without specifying keyword density or length limits.
Filename alone does not replace alt text for accessibility.

cards.title: Order gallery images to answer customer questions
cards.summary: Sequence PDP gallery images — main, alternate angle, details, lifestyle — to match the buyer's questions.
cards.use_when: You are uploading and reordering product images in a PDP gallery.
steps: Start with the main image that shows the product clearly.
Follow with an alternate angle so the buyer can see what the main shot hides.
Then add detailed shots covering specific features and materials buyers will ask about.
Finish with lifestyle images showing the product in context — the source suggests generating lifestyle imagery with AI tools like Gemini if your supplier does not provide them.
Reorder uploaded images so the sequence matches this question-answering flow rather than the order files were captured.
caveats: The source presents this ordering as its usual convention, not a tested ordering that outperforms alternatives for every category.
AI-generated lifestyle images should be checked for accuracy against the actual product.

cards.title: Run a final image checklist before finishing a store
cards.summary: Verify format, size, filenames, alt text and live display before considering product imagery done.
cards.use_when: You have finished uploading and editing a batch of store images and want to confirm nothing was missed.
steps: Confirm every image is a JPEG or PNG and that video content is MP4 rather than GIF.
Confirm each image has been resized and cropped for its layout rather than uploaded straight from a camera.
Confirm files over 500KB have been compressed through a tool such as Tiny SEO or Squash.
Confirm filenames are descriptive, alt text has been written, and gallery order follows main → alternate → detail → lifestyle.
Verify on the live store that images display at the right dimensions and that alt attributes are actually attached, by inspecting image elements.
Re-check any oversized image found during verification, resize it in the customizer, and refresh the page to confirm it renders identically.
caveats: This is a workflow checklist from the source, not a guarantee of specific performance gains.
The 500KB figure is the source's practical threshold for flagging files, not a hard performance ceiling.

cards.title: Inspect rendered image dimensions to find wasted bandwidth
cards.summary: Use browser dev tools to compare an image's intrinsic size to the box it renders in, exposing over-sized assets.
cards.use_when: Store pages feel slow or you suspect imagery is heavier than necessary, and you need evidence before optimizing.
steps: Right-click the suspect image on the live page and choose Inspect.
In the inspector, read the intrinsic dimensions of the image file versus the dimensions of its container.
Flag large gaps as waste — the source's example found a 5,000px-wide image displayed in a 700px box.
Also note the file's total weight where visible; the source's example showed a 6MB section image.
Use the gap to choose the resize target (box width + 100–300px) and then re-check after resizing to confirm the rendered look is unchanged.
Apply the check beyond hero banners to section images and any repeated visual blocks across the store.
caveats: Inspector interfaces vary by browser and change over time — verify the current dev tools layout.
Resizing fixes dimension waste but not compression; a correctly sized file can still be too heavy.

cards.title: Decide whether an image is worth resizing, compressing, or both
cards.summary: Separate dimension waste from weight waste so you apply the right fix to each image.
cards.use_when: You are triaging a catalog of store images and deciding which optimization each file needs.
steps: If dimensions exceed the display box by a wide margin, resize to roughly box size plus 100–300px.
After resizing, check the file weight again — the source reduced a hero from 5,000px to 2,700px and still ended near 1MB, which it judged too much.
If the file remains heavy, compress it; the source estimates the same visual result could come down to about 100KB.
If a file is already correctly sized but still heavy, skip resizing and compress only.
If an image is small and correctly sized, leave it and move on to other assets.
Re-verify visually on the live page after each change so optimization does not degrade the customer's impression of the product.
caveats: The 100KB estimate is the source's illustration, not a target that every image can or should hit.
There is no single fix; the source explicitly pairs resizing with compression for the best result.

cards.title: App Portfolio Triage: Only Keep Apps That Clearly Make Money
cards.summary: App count is a primary Shopify speed lever; install only apps with clear revenue justification and uninstall the rest.
cards.use_when: Auditing installed Shopify apps to decide which to keep, before running a page-speed test.
steps: List every installed app in the Shopify admin and write down the concrete revenue mechanism for each (e.g. sizing chart prevents non-purchase for sized products, review app supplies social proof, subscription app drives recurring orders).
If you cannot state how an app makes money, treat it as a removal candidate — the source's rule is that apps must earn their place.
Prefer apps with many reviews and good reviews, since volume signals the app actually works for other merchants.
Before installing anything new, ask whether native theme features already cover it: announcement bars, discount codes in cart and similar simple elements should not come from an app.

When uninstalling, do not assume cleanup happens: go to Online Store > Themes > Edit code, open theme.liquid, search the app's name and also search the app's store listing name (e.g. a 'free shipping bar' app whose brand is different), remove or comment out leftover script tags with Cmd/Ctrl + /.
Check the customizer's app embeds panel and turn off any embed you are not actively using, then save.
caveats: Apps can still inject assets via Shopify's own script tags, so removing all front-end mentions does not guarantee a specific loading behaviour outside of app embeds being off.
Some apps cannot work defer/async and must stay blocking to keep functionality.

cards.title: Use the Restaurant Analogy to Prioritize Above-the-Fold Loading
cards.summary: Deliver the visible hero first and everything else gradually, mirroring a restaurant bringing drinks before the main course.
cards.use_when: Deciding which storefront assets to prioritize, defer or lazy load on a homepage, landing page or PDP.
steps: Identify everything visible without scrolling: hero banner, logo, main styling, headline copy, hero images, primary product imagery.
Treat these as the 'drinks' — they must render immediately and must not wait for app assets, reward widgets or third-party scripts.
Treat anything below the fold or non-essential (loyalty widgets, chat, extra marketing scripts) as later courses and lazy load or defer them.
Never let a non-essential app asset block the hero: check whether widget assets download before main elements and deprioritize them.
Apply the same priority logic per page type — on a PDP the product image and buy box are the 'drinks'.
caveats: This is a prioritization heuristic, not a measurement; verify the effect with Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights after changes.

cards.title: Defer Script Tags in theme.liquid, Then Fall Back to Async
cards.summary: Add defer to script tags that lack it, test the functionality, and downgrade to async only if defer breaks it.
cards.use_when: Cutting render-blocking JavaScript found in a Shopify theme during a speed optimization pass.
steps: Run a Lighthouse audit (right-click > Inspect > Lighthouse tab) and scroll to the details section to find scripts listed under render-blocking resources.
In Themes > Edit code, open theme.liquid — the file that holds most scripts — and locate script tags missing defer or async.
Add defer so the document loads first and the script loads after; prefer defer over async (the source says defer is better).
Save, load the store, and verify the specific functionality that script powers still works; if yes, keep defer.
If the feature breaks, swap defer for async and re-test; if async also breaks it, leave the script as-is because that script genuinely must block.
Re-run the Lighthouse test to confirm the render-blocking entry disappeared and the score moved (the source saw 78 to 80 after one defer, then 81 after removing a jQuery script).
caveats: You must know what a script does before modifying it — blind defer/async can silently break store functionality.
Score deltas from a single script are small; the source's 1-3 point gains are illustrative of one test, not a guarantee.

cards.title: Self-Host Third-Party Libraries in the Shopify Assets Folder
cards.summary: Replace CDN links for scripts like jQuery with files uploaded to the theme assets folder so the Shopify CDN serves them.
cards.use_when: Adding or keeping a JavaScript library on a store, such as when legacy theme code depends on jQuery.
steps: Open the CDN link in a new browser tab and download the file to your computer.
Upload the file into the theme's assets folder via the code editor.
Reference it the way Shopify does in its own themes: copy an existing script line that uses the asset_url variable and replace only the file name.
Hover the resulting link in the code editor — the tooltip should confirm the asset is served from the Shopify CDN for better performance.
Avoid loading jQuery at all where possible; the source says it is old technology and vanilla JavaScript should replace it — removing a jQuery script raised his test score by one point.
caveats: The source's one-point gain from removing jQuery is a single test observation, not a benchmark.
Only remove a library if you can confirm nothing in the theme depends on it.

cards.title: Understand How Shopify Injects App Scripts via content_for_header
cards.summary: Shopify's injected scripts live behind a content_for_header tag that, when commented out, lifted the source's test from 80% to 100% but breaks apps.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a store's PageSpeed score plateaus despite a lean theme and no active app embeds.
steps: Test with app embeds all turned off in the customizer and still observe a gap between your score and 100 — this isolates Shopify-injected scripts as the cause.
In theme.liquid, locate the content_for_header tag; this is what pulls Shopify's injected scripts into every page load.
The source demonstrates commenting it out and re-running the speed test to confirm the impact (80% jumped to 100% with it disabled).
Never do this on a live theme — the code editor flags it as an error and it will break app and platform functionality.

Instead, if you want the benefit, use a lazy-loading approach for that tag's contents: the source supplies a snippet that defers the injected scripts until user interaction, and he measured 97% and an overall claim of 10-20% gain over the current score.
caveats: The 10-20% claim is the presenter's own estimate; he also warns the technique has small impact if the store has larger underlying speed problems.
This is a third-party snippet, not an official Shopify feature — verify current Shopify behaviour before relying on it.

cards.title: Compress and Resize Product and Hero Images Before Upload
cards.summary: Replace multi-megabyte source images with compressed files, keeping the whole store's media around 2-3 MB.
cards.use_when: Preparing hero banners, category images and product photography for upload to a Shopify store.
steps: Check the file size of every image you plan to upload; the source found an 8 MB hero image on a student's store and treats 2-3 MB as the target for the entire store.
Resize first: open the image in a tool like Photopea, go to Image > Size, and set the resolution to around 2,000 px, which the source treats as sufficient.
Export as JPEG at roughly 70% quality (lower is acceptable if quality holds).
Optionally run the result through a compressor like TinyPNG/TinyJPEG; the source's example only saved a further 8% after a good export, so the export step did most of the work.
Do a visual side-by-side comparison — the source's compressed 234 KB file looked indistinguishable from the 8 MB original, and a 100 KB file matched a 400 KB one.
If manual work per image is impractical, use a bulk image-compression app in Shopify instead.
caveats: Some themes automatically re-serve smaller derivatives of large uploads, but you should still compress before uploading rather than relying on that.
The source's file-size targets come from his own practice, not a published standard.

cards.title: Set Image Upload Dimensions Slightly Above the Container Size
cards.summary: Upload images 100-300 px wider than the container box to avoid blurriness without oversizing the file.
cards.use_when: Configuring image width settings for a section or theme setting, such as a 700 px hero container.
steps: Find the actual rendered box width — the source's example box is 700 px.
Set the image dimension to roughly 100-300 px above the box width (he used about 1000 px for a 700 px box) rather than uploading at exactly the box size.
Uploading exactly matching dimensions risks a blurry rendering; uploading far larger wastes file size.
Apply the setting, refresh the storefront and confirm the image still renders identically.
Inspect the element to verify the served width reflects your setting.
This setting is available in the theme editor and can be docked to the side while you work.
caveats: The 100-300 px margin is the source's working rule of thumb, not a measured optimum; check the visual result.

cards.title: Match Image Format to Use: JPEG Default, PNG for Transparency, MP4 Over GIF
cards.summary: Use JPEG for photos, PNG only when transparency is genuinely needed, and HTML video tags with MP4 instead of GIFs.
cards.use_when: Choosing file formats when preparing product images, logos and motion assets for a store.
steps: Default to JPEG and compress it for every photographic image.
Use PNG only when you need something cropped out or transparent, such as a logo overlaid on a background.
Never use GIFs — the source says they are huge; if you need motion or an animation, embed an MP4 inside an HTML video tag, which loads much faster.
Apply the same compression discipline to video files as to images; oversized video is equally damaging.
Treat 'media' decisions as a per-page-type choice: hero video, PDP gallery images and category thumbnails all follow the same format rules.
caveats: Format choice does not substitute for compression — a large JPEG can still be worse than a reasonable PNG.

cards.title: Preload Above-the-Fold Media and Lazy Load Everything Below
cards.summary: Tell the browser which media matters (preload, no lazy loading, no animation) and defer the rest until scroll.
cards.use_when: Setting loading behaviour on hero banners, above-the-fold product imagery and long-page sections.
steps: Mark every asset visible without scrolling as preloaded so the browser gives it priority.
Lazy load everything underneath the fold so it downloads only when the customer scrolls to it.
Do not use animations or transitions on the hero — an animation forces the browser to download an effects library before displaying the image, delaying the hero.
If LCP readings are large, inspect the main image for fade-ins, slide-ins or similar effects and remove them.
Lazy load app widgets that are not essential to the buying process, using lazy sizes or loading="lazy" attributes where appropriate, and keep essential buying-flow assets eager.
caveats: Preload too many assets and you recreate the problem you are solving; apply it to above-the-fold only.
The source notes that a slider's first image specifically must not be lazy loaded or animated.

cards.title: Trim Custom Font Variations and Enable font-display: swap
cards.summary: Reduce custom font weights/styles to essentials and add swap so text renders before the font downloads.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a designed Shopify theme that ships custom typography, or troubleshooting rendering delays on text.
steps: Inventory which font weights and styles actually appear on the storefront.
Limit yourself to roughly three variations of a custom font; the source recommends no more than three and calls five or ten variations 'not a great idea'.
In Themes > Edit code, search for the @font-face declarations that import your custom fonts.
Ensure each imported font has the font-display: swap property so the browser shows fallback text and swaps the custom font in once downloaded.
If the design does not genuinely require custom fonts, use the fonts built into Shopify themes instead — the source considers them good enough for most stores.
caveats: The three-variation limit is the source's own recommendation, not a platform rule.
font-display swap can cause a visible flash of fallback text; whether that trade-off is acceptable is a design judgement.

cards.title: Choose a Simpler Theme Over a Feature-Rich One Unless Features Pay
cards.summary: Premium and feature-heavy themes ship unused libraries; free themes like Dawn and Horizon are the better default unless data justifies otherwise.
cards.use_when: Selecting a theme for a new Shopify store or deciding whether to upgrade from a free theme.
steps: Default to a simple free theme; the source names Dawn and Horizon as the best starting points and warns against going for the most complex premium theme.
Do not buy a premium theme for pop-ups or features on a hunch or because a video recommended it — require a clear reason it will make more money.
If you genuinely expect to use specific features and expect them to drive revenue, a premium theme is justified.
When evaluating, remember that the extra libraries and options you never use still load and cost performance.
Note that effect-heavy designs delay display because effects libraries must load first.
Choosing a free theme also saves roughly $300 versus a premium theme, according to the source.
caveats: The $300 saving figure and the free-theme recommendation are the presenter's guidance for beginners and lean stores, not a rule for all businesses.

cards.title: Weigh Migrating an Old Theme vs. Rebuilding on Dawn or Horizon
cards.summary: Rebuilding an established but slow theme on a modern base can be cheaper than continuously patching outdated technology.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to keep optimizing a legacy Shopify theme or migrate the store.
steps: If the store is established and cannot change theme, implement the levers in order: app audit, script defer, image compression, font trimming — these are still possible on older themes.
Accept that some fixes get technical on old themes because the technology is outdated and the theme was not built for speed.
If you have the option and the theme is the bottleneck, build the site again on Dawn or Horizon; you must rebuild every section because structure differs, but a lighter newer theme loads fewer files.
Compare the cost of repeatedly optimizing an ageing theme against the one-off cost of rebuilding — the source says optimizing an older theme can end up costing more.
Plan migrations around other store changes (redesign, revamp) rather than as an isolated emergency project.
caveats: A migration requires rebuilding sections, apps and customizations — budget for that disruption.
The source gives no hard timeline for when a theme must be retired.

cards.title: Recognize That Most Free Shopify Themes Are the Same Codebase
cards.summary: Twenty-three free themes reduce to two codebases — thirteen Dawn variants and ten Horizon variants — differing only in settings and JSON.
cards.use_when: Choosing between free Shopify themes or deciding whether switching to a differently-styled free theme changes performance.
steps: In the theme store, filter for free themes and note the badges dividing Dawn-based from Horizon-based themes.
Understand that picking among variants of the same base changes only styling, images, colours and settings — the codebase is identical.
Check theme version numbers: all Dawn-based themes share one version (the source saw 1.5.3.0) and all Horizon-based themes share another (1.0.1).
Conclusion for selection: do not expect a performance or capability change from switching between two themes built on the same base — choose on fit and design.
If you want Horizon's structural capabilities, you must move to a Horizon-based theme, not a Dawn variant.
caveats: Version numbers and store badges change over time — verify the current theme-store labelling.
This applies to free themes at the time of the source, not necessarily to paid themes or future releases.

cards.title: Understand Horizon's Global Blocks vs. Dawn's Section-Scoped Blocks
cards.summary: Horizon lets blocks be reused across any block-accepting section, while Dawn restricts each section to its own block list.
cards.use_when: Designing a storefront layout and deciding how much free-form composition you need from the theme.
steps: On a Dawn-based theme, adding a section (e.g. image with text) shows only the blocks permitted for that section; blocks cannot move between sections.
On a Horizon-based theme, sections that accept blocks accept global blocks; click Add block and see a much larger shared list (logo, accordion and more).
Global blocks themselves can contain sub-blocks — an accordion added as a block gets its own nested block options.
Check the theme's code editor: Horizon-based themes add a blocks folder alongside templates, holding the global blocks; Dawn has templates only.
Use this as the deciding factor when choosing between simple versus composable layouts — more flexibility means more layout options but also more to configure.
caveats: Block availability and nesting behaviour are theme-version dependent; verify in your own customizer.
Customizer improvements such as copy-paste of sections and renaming apply to all themes, not just Horizon.

cards.title: Benchmark Theme Speed With an Apples-to-Apples Comparison
cards.summary: The source tested identical stores on Horizon and Dawn with app embeds off, getting 71/74 for Horizon and 56/78 for Dawn.
cards.use_when: Justifying a theme migration decision or setting performance expectations before rebuilding a store.
steps: Set up the two themes on one store with identical customizations — the source used a hero banner and a few products only.
Turn off all app embeds in the customizer for both themes so uninstalled/unused apps do not distort the comparison.
Run PageSpeed Insights on both storefront URLs and record mobile and desktop scores plus LCP and blocking-time details.
In the source's test, Horizon scored 71 mobile / 74 desktop and Dawn scored 56 mobile / 78 desktop — his conclusion was Horizon is somewhat better overall.
Read the diagnostics rather than only the headline number: the LCP in his test came from an oversized hero image, so compression was the next fix for both.
caveats: Single-run results are noisy and store-specific — treat these numbers as an example, not a benchmark you can expect to reproduce.
The comparison held apps inactive; a real store's app mix will change the outcome.

cards.title: Keep Dawn for Now; Build New Stores on Horizon
cards.summary: The source advises not rushing a Dawn-to-Horizon migration since Horizon is young, but says Horizon is likely the future standard.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to migrate an existing Shopify store to Horizon during a redesign or a new-build decision.
steps: For an existing Dawn store with significant work invested, keep Dawn — the source says there is no reason to rush and cites merchants still running the much older Debut theme successfully.
Note that Shopify stopped releasing updates to Dawn earlier in the year, and the source does not expect Dawn to adopt the new structure.
If you are building a new store, go with Horizon or a Horizon-based free theme.
