If you will redesign or revamp anyway, do it on Horizon at that point rather than as a standalone migration.
Wait for maturity: the source observed Horizon already at version 1.0.1 with a patch pushed, and expects early bugs to be ironed out.
caveats: This is the presenter's forward-looking opinion about theme roadmaps, not an official Shopify statement.
He flagged that Dawn would likely be sunset eventually but explicitly not imminently.

cards.title: Diagnose CLS by Reading Google's Rendering Screenshots
cards.summary: Compare PageSpeed Insights' captured screenshots frame by frame to identify which element pushes layout down.
cards.use_when: Investigating a poor layout-stability score on a storefront that loads but shifts while users interact.
steps: Run PageSpeed Insights and open the rendering/screenshot sequence Google captured during load.
Compare consecutive frames to spot elements that appear suddenly and push content down, around or larger.
Note that GIF motion in the capture is expected if the store uses GIFs, but the real signal is an element appearing between frames.
Note the suspect element's on-page ID, inspect it on the storefront and search the document to trace its source.

Elements injected after load usually come from apps — the source identified a free-shipping-bar app (Hexom) creating CLS; he calls such simple announcement bars something themes already provide, so an app for it is unnecessary.
Check the desktop tab too: the source found one site with zero CLS on mobile but a large desktop reading, and his free-shipping-bar example was worse on desktop.
caveats: The source ranks CLS as the most impactful metric in his experience, ahead of LCP — this is his qualitative ranking, not a Google-published weight.
Fixing LCP and CLS alone moved his illustrative store above 50, possibly 60 — a case observation, not a benchmark.

cards.title: Fix LCP by Un-lazy-loading and De-animating the Hero Image
cards.summary: The largest contentful paint is usually the hero; it must load eagerly with no lazy attribute, no fade-in and maximum compression.
cards.use_when: Improving a poor LCP reading on a homepage, category page or any page where a large hero dominates.
steps: Identify the largest element — typically the hero banner image or the first slide of a slider.
Remove loading="lazy" and any lazy-sizes classes or loading-lazy patterns from that image; the source says this should never be lazy loaded.
Set loading="eager" instead, telling the browser the image is important and should load as fast as possible.
Remove fade-in, slide-in or other entrance effects from that image, since effects force an effects library download before the image shows.
Compress the image as much as you can once the loading behaviour is correct.
In a slider, implement logic so the first image is never lazy loaded or animated while later slides can be; also check blocking time, which affects LCP too.
caveats: In his example the image was lazy loaded and should have said eager — but LCP can also be driven by blocking time and effects, so check more than the loading attribute.

cards.title: Decide Whether Your Store Actually Needs a Good Speed Score
cards.summary: Speed scores matter for organic acquisition; stores driving all traffic with ad budget can convert without them.
cards.use_when: Setting speed-optimization priorities and budget for a store before committing technical work.
steps: Assess your traffic mix: if you have a large ad budget and depend on paid traffic rather than organic, tight speed scores are less critical — the source notes big brands with lower scores still sell a lot.
If you rely on or want organic traffic from Google, prioritise the PageSpeed Insights score and fix the flagged items, especially LCP and CLS.
Separate the customer-experience case from the SEO case: the source's buying-impulse argument is that customers arrive from ads, hit a slow page and bounce within 2-3 seconds.
If you have visits but no purchases, treat speed as a candidate explanation worth testing rather than assuming it is the only cause.
Sequence your effort: fix LCP and CLS first, since the source says these two alone can move a poor score into the 50s-60s in his experience.
caveats: The '2-3 second' expectation is the presenter's own behaviour as a shopper and his model of customer behaviour, not a measured threshold.
The claim that optimized Shopify stores get more sales is his observation from years of client work, not a controlled study.

cards.title: Search a Downloaded Theme Folder for Residual App and Pixel Code
cards.summary: Download the theme, open it in a free code editor and search across all files for app names, pixels and libraries you no longer use.
cards.use_when: Deep-cleaning a storefront's code after uninstalling apps or removing tracking, beyond what theme.liquid search reveals.
steps: In the Shopify admin go to Themes > Download theme and send it to your email; save and unzip it locally.
Install a code editor such as Cursor (free) and open the unzipped theme folder as a project.
Use the editor's global search to query an app's brand name, and also its listing name — a two-part name means two searches.
When a match appears (the source's example found a match inside a JSON file), open it and inspect the reference.
Repeat for old pixels and libraries, e.g. searching a leftover analytics provider name shows every file that still references it.
Checking file by file in the theme editor is slow, so use the global search as the efficient route.
caveats: A downloaded copy is a snapshot — re-download if you have since changed the theme.
Reading matches still requires judgement about whether removing them is safe.

cards.title: Audit Shopify theme files for leftover app code with a code editor
cards.summary: Open the theme export in a code editor and search for app names to find and remove residual pixel and tracking code slowing the store.
cards.use_when: Store speed work is blocked or polluted by old app scripts you can no longer control from the Shopify admin, and you need to locate the exact theme file and line before deleting anything.
steps: Download your theme (Online Store > Themes > ... > Download theme file) and unzip it, or open it directly in a code editor such as Cursor (free; has AI assistance if you don't write code) using Open Folder.
Use the editor's global search to find app keywords, e.g. 'hexom' for an uninstalled app, 'Google' for Google-related tags, or 'logs' for a reviews app. See which files contain them.
When you open a match, note the file name and the approximate line number (e.g. a pixel at line 72 of a .json or .liquid file).
Back in Shopify, go to Theme > Edit code, search the same file, jump to the nearby line, and remove only the target tag/code.
Save and verify the store still works before doing the next removal; only remove code you have positively matched to an app you no longer use.
caveats: Editing live theme code can break functionality or checkout; test after each change and keep a downloaded backup of the original theme.
The source stresses confirming what a script does before altering it, because some apps require their scripts to load immediately.

cards.title: Find and compress oversized non-product images in Shopify Files
cards.summary: Audit the Shopify content/files library for multi-megabyte images, then resize and compress them to under ~1 MB before re-uploading to their sections.
cards.use_when: Store images hurt page speed and app-based image compressors only touch product photos, leaving homepage/section banners heavy.
steps: In Shopify go to Content > Files and sort through the media library looking for large offenders (e.g. 3 MB, 5 MB). The presenter's working target: total page weight around 2–3 MB, and individual images under 1 MB, ideally a few hundred KB.
Identify which theme sections use each heavy image, then download it.

Resize large images (e.g. reduce width to ~1500px, keeping aspect ratio) if a compression pass alone still leaves them over budget; the presenter's example went from ~5 MB to ~1.6 MB after resize, then to ~400 KB after compression.
Run the downloaded file through a free compression site (the demo used one that cut size by roughly 50–70%) and download the compressed output.
Re-upload the compressed image to the same section/file so the reference is preserved, and replace the original wherever it appears.
caveats: Compression targets are the presenter's heuristics, not Google thresholds; balance quality against weight for hero imagery.
Always keep the original if you may need higher resolution later.

cards.title: Choose JPEG vs PNG vs GIF for store imagery
cards.summary: Upload JPEG for photos because they compress best, reserve PNG for overlay graphics needing transparency, and avoid GIFs entirely for performance.
cards.use_when: Deciding export/upload format for product photos, section banners, or overlay graphics that affect page weight.
steps: For standard photos (product shots, lifestyle banners) export and upload as JPEG — the source says JPEGs compress much better and yield lower file sizes than PNGs.
Use PNG only when you need transparency, e.g. decorative bubbles/graphics overlaid on a product or spanning sections where the background must show through.
Never use GIF: the source calls GIFs bad for performance and unprofessional-looking, and notes big brands avoid them.
For any looping background video, use an MP4 file set to autoplay/loop rather than an animated GIF.
caveats: The 'never use GIF / big brands never do' claim is the presenter's opinion, stated as such; style choices may vary, but the performance point on GIF weight stands.
Switching a transparent graphic to JPEG will lose the transparency effect.

cards.title: Lazy-load below-the-fold images but never the hero image
cards.summary: Apply lazy loading to off-screen images to cut initial download, while forcing the main hero/in-view image to load eagerly to protect LCP.
cards.use_when: Setting theme image behavior or debugging slow perceived load / poor LCP on homepage banners and product grids.
steps: Leave the main hero image (the banner at the top) loading eagerly — do not lazy-load it, because in-view images are usually the Largest Contentful Paint element and lazy-loading them worsens LCP, which the source says Google dislikes.
Apply lazy loading (loading="lazy") to everything below the fold: lower section images, secondary product images, and decorative overlays.
If your theme's hero section lazy-loads its first image by default, add custom logic to exempt that first image so it renders immediately.
Verify behavior in the browser/network panel: the in-view images should download right away, with further images downloading only as the user scrolls.
caveats: The presenter cautions that if you already have serious LCP or CLS problems, lazy-loading fixes won't be enough — those issues need separate attention.
Theme behavior differs by theme version; verify the current interface and default markup.

cards.title: Add font-display: swap to custom fonts to avoid render blocking
cards.summary: Find @font-face rules in theme files and add font-display: swap so text renders in a fallback font until the custom font downloads.
cards.use_when: Custom store fonts create render-blocking delay and you want layout to paint immediately on slow connections.
steps: In your theme code (via the code editor), search for '@font-face' across all theme files — this is how fonts get imported.
For each @font-face rule, check whether it has a font-display: swap property; if not, add it (e.g. just below the font-family declaration).
Save and test: on a simulated slow connection (e.g. 3G in devtools) you should see a standard browser font render first, then swap to the custom font once it downloads.
Accept the brief 'font swap' flash as the trade-off: the document no longer waits for the font before rendering, removing blocking time.
caveats: Without swap, the whole document can be blocked until the font downloads, creating significant blocking time — this is the problem being fixed.
On fast connections the swap may be invisible, so test under throttling to confirm it works.

cards.title: Add async or defer to third-party scripts after checking their purpose
cards.summary: Inspect scripts in theme.liquid, determine what each does, then add async or defer to non-critical ones to stop them blocking the theme.
cards.use_when: Third-party scripts (jQuery, libraries, or app scripts) sit in theme.liquid and load synchronously, slowing first render.
steps: Open theme.liquid and scan for <script> tags, including ones you don't recognize (added by apps or a previous developer).
Investigate what each script does and how it works before touching it — you must know its dependency on load order.
Add 'async' to allow the script to download alongside the theme; add 'defer' to make it download only after the theme fully loads.
Save and re-test; some solutions/apps specifically cannot use async or defer because they need their scripts immediately, so keep those untouched.
caveats: The source says most (not all) theme scripts can take async/defer — verify app requirements, since loading a required script late can break functionality (e.g. consent, checkout widgets).
Differentiating async vs defer matters for scripts that depend on DOM readiness.

cards.title: Defer all app scripts until user interaction to cut blocking time
cards.summary: Replace Shopify's async-load app-script loader with a snippet that injects app scripts only after the user scrolls, clicks, or otherwise interacts, improving blocking-time metrics.
cards.use_when: Many installed apps load their scripts immediately and inflate blocking time; you want to prioritize first paint over third-party app JS.
steps: In devtools, inspect the <head> and find the 'async load' function that injects scripts for all installed apps — it runs concurrently with your theme.
Comment out that async-load block in the theme's content file (the source uses comment tags around it).
Paste the provided lazy-load snippet (in the video description) directly beneath the commented-out block; it defers injecting app scripts until the user starts interacting (scroll, click).
Save and re-run a speed test after a short wait so the change propagates. In the demo the score moved from roughly 40–50 to ~85 after the change and reverted when removed.
Also go to Customize > App embeds and turn off any app embeds you don't actively use before testing.
caveats: The code is not as effective if you have high CLS or LCP — those issues take priority over blocking time.
The demo's 40–50 → ~85 jump is a single case example, not a guarantee; results depend on your app mix and theme.
Verify the current theme file name and interface before editing; theme markup changes over time.

cards.title: Prune unused apps and app embeds to reduce third-party load
cards.summary: Uninstall apps you don't actively use and disable unused app embeds, since third-party app code on external servers is a major Shopify speed drag.
cards.use_when: Auditing store speed when many apps are installed, or deciding whether a low-value app is worth keeping.
steps: List installed apps and remove any you aren't currently using — the source's rule: if unsure, uninstall; you can reinstall later.
Keep only apps that bring clear value to you or your customer, since app code lives on third-party servers and its quality can't be controlled.
Go to theme Customize > App embeds and turn off any embeds that are enabled but not needed.
Re-test speed after pruning to see the combined effect.
caveats: Too many apps can make a store unusable, per the source — but some apps are load-bearing; confirm before removing.
App embed locations and menus may change in the current Shopify admin; verify the interface.

cards.title: Plan a three-keyword SEO scheme per page with Google Keyword Planner
cards.summary: Assign one main and two secondary keywords to each page, balancing search volume, competition, and buyer intent, before editing any page content.
cards.use_when: Beginning store SEO work — planning which keywords the homepage, product, and collection pages should target.
steps: Brainstorm keywords that represent your brand and products, then validate them in Google Keyword Planner (requires a Google Ads account; under Tools > Planning).

Enter a seed term (e.g. 'homemade soap'), set country/language, and read results: monthly search volume, competition, and CPC (in the demo, 'homemade soap' showed 1k–10k searches and bids of $0.20–$1.54).
Pick a sensible main keyword plus two supporting keywords per page, favoring ones with buying intent (e.g. 'homemade soap for sale') over purely informational ones (e.g. 'how to make homemade soap').
Use the 'start with website' feature on a competitor's URL to see the keywords they rank for and borrow ideas.
Cross-check volume/intent in free tools (Google Trends + Glimpse extension, or Google autocomplete predictions) and confirm in Keyword Planner before committing.
caveats: Volume/competition/CPC figures are the source's tool examples, not universal benchmarks; niches differ.
Paid tools (Ahrefs, Semrush) give extra intent/depth but aren't required — Keyword Planner is the free baseline.

cards.title: Optimize the store-level SEO title and meta description
cards.summary: Set the main keyword in the site title and supporting keywords plus a call-to-action in the meta description so the brand's search listing earns clicks.
cards.use_when: Configuring the global store-level search listing (Online Store > Preferences > Search engine listing) that represents your brand in search results.
steps: Go to Online Store > Preferences > Search engine listing.
Put the chosen main keyword in the title field and supporting keywords (plus a call to action) in the description field.
Keep the title within the character limit shown (the demo used 63 of 70 characters) and make sure the keywords genuinely represent your brand and niche — avoid too-broad or off-niche terms.
Have ChatGPT draft title/description from your keywords, then refine for brand voice and save; verify the listing reflects your store before publishing.
caveats: The source notes many Shopify owners neglect these fields, but avoid keyword stuffing terms that don't represent the store.
Meta description length guidance here is the presenter's; search engines may rewrite snippets anyway.

cards.title: Rename generic product titles into keyword-rich H1 titles
cards.summary: Convert vague product names into descriptive, keyword-bearing titles, and test keyword candidates in Keyword Planner before finalizing.
cards.use_when: Product titles are vague (e.g. a cute name that says nothing to search engines) and need to become the page's explanatory H1.
steps: On a product page, the product title is the page's main H1 and explains to Google what the page is about; a name like 'sweet honey bomb' tells Google nothing — reinforce this by rewriting it.
Copy the product's spec/description and ask ChatGPT for high-volume keyword candidates for that kind of product.
Validate the promising candidates in Keyword Planner, keeping ones with good volume; discard the weak ones.
Feed the validated keywords back to ChatGPT and have it generate several title options containing at least the main keyword; pick/tweak the best.
Paste the new title into the product, save, and adjust theme title font size in the customizer if the longer title looks oversized.
caveats: Ensure the title still accurately represents the product and the brand; don't force keywords that misdescribe the item.
Keyword volumes are tool figures and change over time/region.

cards.title: Write substantive 100–400 word product and collection descriptions
cards.summary: Replace bare spec dumps with keyword-inclusive, human-sounding descriptions of at least 100 words (300–400 ideal) to give search engines crawlable content.
cards.use_when: Product pages or collection pages have thin descriptions (just specs, or none) and need indexable, keyword-rich copy.
steps: Gather the product's specs/attributes and use ChatGPT to generate a description based on them, instructing it to include keywords found in Keyword Planner.
Ensure the text sounds human and doesn't read as obviously AI-generated; format with bold, images, etc.
Meet the length target: the source says at least 100 words, and 300–400 is ideal — copying only specs is a common mistake.
For collection pages, add a description (100–400 words) with the right keywords; if you don't want it pushing products down, move it below the product grid.
Save. Collection descriptions matter for ranking even when placed lower on the page.
caveats: The 100-word minimum and 300–400 ideal are the presenter's guidance, not an official ranking rule.
Long keyword-stuffed copy can look dull without images — balance readability against keyword coverage.

cards.title: Write alt text and rename image files for SEO and accessibility
cards.summary: Add descriptive alt text and human-readable file names using target keywords and image angle to every product and section image.
cards.use_when: Product images and site/section images have gibberish file names or no alt text and you want better indexing and accessibility.
steps: On a product image, write alt text that combines the target keyword, the actual product, key attributes, and the angle (e.g. '[keyword] bath bomb purple frontal').
Rename the underlying file to match that descriptive alt text instead of a numeric/gibberish name.
Repeat for all images in the product media gallery.
For section images, go to Content > Files, open each media item, add descriptive alt text, and rename the file — most library files will be gibberish by default.
Verify in the product listing (inspect the image) that the URL now reflects the descriptive name.
caveats: The source notes this also aids visually impaired users and that Google rewards the practice.
Doing this manually is impractical for very large catalogs — the source points to an automation app instead.

cards.title: Set SEO-friendly URL handles with automatic redirects
cards.summary: Rewrite product and collection handles into keyword-rich slugs and keep the automatic redirect checked so old links don't 404.
cards.use_when: Product or collection URLs are vague or non-descriptive and you're finalizing on-page SEO for those pages.
steps: In the product/collection's search engine listing section, replace the URL handle with the title (drop grammar/special characters — handles don't need them).
Keep the automatic redirect option checked so the old URL forwards to the new one.
Save; bookmarkers of the old link will be redirected instead of hitting a 404, protecting conversions.
Apply the same handle cleanup to collections, whose handles are often wrong or generic.
caveats: Only unchecked redirects cause lost traffic/404s — the source stresses leaving the redirect enabled whenever you change a handle.
Changing handles has SEO implications; keep them stable once set.

cards.title: Ensure each page has exactly one H1 tag
cards.summary: Check that every page (home, product, collection) has a single H1, since multiple H1s confuse Google's understanding of the page.
cards.use_when: Auditing on-page SEO structure, especially after adding custom sections a developer built that may have introduced extra H1s.
steps: Inspect the page in devtools to confirm which element is the H1: on Shopify Dawn, the homepage H1 is the logo, a collection page's H1 is the collection title, and a product page's H1 is the product title.
Scan custom sections for stray H1 tags — a developer-built or DIY section might use an H1 that competes with the real page H1.
If two H1s describe different things, Google can't tell which is authoritative; demote the extra ones to H2/H3.
Enforce one H1 per page across product, collection, and content pages.
caveats: Confirmed for the Dawn theme by the presenter; other themes may structure H1s differently, so inspect rather than assume.
Don't rely on visual size — the H1 may be the logo or a heading you didn't expect.

cards.title: Write 160-character meta descriptions for click-through
cards.summary: Craft per-page meta descriptions around ~160 characters focused on enticing clicks rather than keyword density.
cards.use_when: Finalizing a product or blog post's search engine listing meta description.
steps: At the bottom of the product/page editor, open the search engine listing and view the meta description (the product page can show an excerpt automatically).
If the auto-excerpt reads well, you can leave it — especially for large catalogs where manual edits are impractical.
Otherwise, take the product description and ask ChatGPT for a ~160-character meta description, then paste and save.
Prioritize persuasion over keyword density here: the meta description's job is to make searchers click, more so than the page title/body copy.
caveats: The source explicitly says you don't need keywords as heavily here as in the title/description — focus on click appeal.
Search engines may override the description; the ~160-character figure is a guideline.

cards.title: Use internal linking to speed up crawling and discovery
cards.summary: Link products to blog posts and other pages within content so Googlebot discovers and indexes pages faster.
cards.use_when: Building blog content or benefit/education pages and planning how they connect to product and collection pages.
steps: Within blog posts and content pages, add links to the relevant products (e.g. a page describing a product's benefits should link to that product).
Add links wherever you legitimately can across the site — from pages to products, blog posts to collections, etc.
This helps Google discover more pages faster, because crawling one page reveals the next, which then gets crawled too.
caveats: Link contextually and relevantly; the source frames it as helping discovery, not as a trick for arbitrary link volume.
Blog posts each have their own title/content/search-listing fields that should also be optimized.

cards.title: Verify mobile friendliness before treating SEO as complete
cards.summary: Preview the store as a mobile device to confirm layout, text, and images render correctly, since Google downranks non-mobile-friendly stores.
cards.use_when: Pre-launch or SEO audit checklist step to confirm mobile rendering, which Google factors into authority/ranking.
steps: In Chrome, right-click > Inspect, then toggle the device toolbar and pick a device (e.g. iPhone 12 Pro) to preview the store.
In Safari, use Develop > Enter Responsive Design to preview mobile rendering.
Check that text stays within the viewport, images aren't shrunken/distorted, and everything is reachable.
If it all renders well, you pass the mobile-friendliness check and can move to the next step (speed).
caveats: Most modern Shopify themes are mobile-friendly out of the box, per the source, but verifying is still worthwhile.
This is a visual/devtools check, not a formal Lighthouse category.

cards.title: Use PageSpeed Insights for a baseline and install speed snippets
cards.summary: Run Google PageSpeed Insights to gauge loading speed, understand its 28-day rolling data, and apply snippets for incremental gains.
cards.use_when: Establishing a speed baseline or checking whether recent changes improved performance.
steps: Enter your URL on Google's PageSpeed Insights and click Analyze to get a page score plus field/historical data.
Note that the historical graphs reflect the past 28 days, so a fix done today won't fully show in those graphs for ~28 days.
Use the results to prioritize: loading speed is complex, and you need to fix most flagged issues to rank well.
Apply speed-boost snippets (the source offers them) that the presenter claims can boost store speed by ~10–20%, per his own stores.
caveats: The 10–20% snippet boost is the presenter's claim, not a guaranteed result.
Field data lagging 28 days means you can't judge a fix from the field graphs immediately — use lab results in the meantime.

cards.title: Add rich snippets to earn larger search listings
cards.summary: Implement structured data (product, FAQ, article snippets) so listings show ratings, prices, availability, or FAQ answers and draw more clicks.
cards.use_when: Search result listings look plain and you want a bigger, richer presence (FAQ dropdowns, product ratings/prices) under your link.
steps: Determine the snippet type that fits a page: FAQ/Q&A for blog posts answering a question, product snippets for products, article snippets for posts.
Add the corresponding structured data — this requires custom code or an app (the source links a guide and an app that does it).
For product snippets, include description, rating, number of reviews, price, and availability so the listing shows these visually.
Once rich snippets are live, your listing can occupy more vertical space (even multiple products), attracting more clicks than plain competitors.
caveats: Requires custom code or an app; markup must match real page data (accurate prices/ratings) to be eligible.
The source frames click advantage as the goal; it isn't a guarantee of ranking gains.

cards.title: Publish keyword-researched content at least twice a month
cards.summary: Maintain a content cadence (2–4 posts/month) on topics close to your products, researched in Keyword Planner, to feed Google fresh relevant content.
cards.use_when: Planning an ongoing SEO content strategy to keep the store's pages fresh and discoverable.
steps: Plan at least two posts a month, ideally four (one per week).
Research post topics using Keyword Planner and write about topics close to what you sell and that your customers want to learn about.

For each post, set a title containing a main and secondary keyword, write valuable description/body text containing the keywords, and complete the search engine listing with an enticing ~160-character meta description.
Give the post a URL handle containing the title's keywords so Google understands the page.
Optionally connect the post with internal links to relevant products.
caveats: The 2–4 posts/month cadence is the presenter's recommendation, not a rule Google enforces.
Content still needs to be genuinely useful and relevant to the niche.

cards.title: Earn backlinks from authoritative sites and partners
cards.summary: Get featured on high-authority websites, influencer posts, or partner blogs linking to your store to inherit credibility and rank higher.
cards.use_when: Building off-page SEO and authority for a store competing for higher search placement.
steps: Identify authoritative websites, influencers, or friendly partners who can mention your store.
Arrange for them to write about your store and include a link to it.
Paying attention to partner authority matters: links from authoritative sites let your store gain some of that authority, increasing trustworthiness and ranking chances.
caveats: The source frames backlinks as building trust/authority; link quality/authority matters more than volume.
No specific quantity benchmark is given.

cards.title: Set a primary domain and submit your sitemap to Search Console
cards.summary: Configure one primary domain, then submit the Shopify sitemap in Google Search Console so Google crawls and indexes the store.
cards.use_when: After on-page SEO is complete, kickstarting Google crawling and indexing of the store.
steps: In Settings > Domains, ensure a single primary domain is set (a premium/custom domain, not the myshopify one) so Google knows which URLs to crawl — do this before submitting the sitemap.
Load your sitemap by appending /sitemap.xml to your store URL and copy that URL.
Create/link your property in Google Search Console, then go to Indexing > Sitemaps and submit the sitemap URL.
Google will begin crawling and indexing the store's pages.
caveats: If you set the primary domain after submitting, you can submit a new sitemap; getting the primary domain right first avoids confusion.
The exact Search Console menus can change; verify the current interface.

cards.title: Submit Sitemap and Set Primary Domain Before Google Indexing
cards.summary: Connect Search Console, submit your sitemap, and fix your Shopify primary domain so Google crawls the correct URLs.
cards.use_when: Preparing a new or neglected Shopify store for organic search indexing before investing in on-page SEO or content.
steps: Link your store property to Google Search Console and open Indexing > Sitemaps.
Paste your store's sitemap URL and hit Submit; Google will then start crawling and indexing store pages.
Before submitting, go to Settings > Domains and confirm which domain should be primary. Stores with a custom domain often show multiple entries (the .myshopify.com plus the custom).
Set the premium/custom domain as primary (not the myshopify URL). Do this first, then submit the sitemap so Google crawls the right URLs; if you already submitted, resubmit after switching.

Also fill in brand information (logo, colors) under the brand tab — Search Console won't use it, but Facebook, Google and other sales channels pull it to represent you better when your products syndicate.
caveats: Shopify admin menus and Search Console interface change; verify current panel names before following.

cards.title: Brand Asset Completeness for Sales Channel Syndication
cards.summary: Fill in store brand info so product feeds to Facebook and Google represent your store accurately.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing a store that feeds products into Facebook, Google Shopping or other sales channels.
steps: Locate the brand settings tab (in the source, found via Shopify Sidekick because the menu position wasn't obvious).
Upload logos and define brand colors there.

This matters because external channels like Facebook and Google pull this information and use it when representing your products and store, so incomplete brand data means weaker, inconsistent presentation off-site.
Treat this as a prerequisite feed-quality step alongside product data, not a design nicety.
caveats: The source couldn't recall the exact menu path; use search/Sidekick or check current Shopify admin navigation.

cards.title: Use an SEO App Dashboard to Drive Pages Toward 100% Score
cards.summary: Install an SEO app (e.g. SEOAnt) that scores pages and points to exact fixes, then work issues one by one to raise page scores.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to buy an SEO tool and how to systematize on-page optimization across many product and collection pages.
steps: Install an SEO app from the Shopify App Store (source demos 'SEOAnt' / AI SEO). It shows a store speed score and an SEO summary flagging issues such as uncompressed images.
Work the flagged issues directly in the app dashboard instead of hunting them manually.
Open a product page's breakdown and enter the target keywords you were aiming for; the score rises if you're actually targeting those keywords (source saw 80% after targeting two keywords).

Fix the specific pointers: add an H2 in the description (source pasted the product title again and marked it H2, lifting 80% to 91), add 1-4 images inside the description, and include the target keyword in the meta description.
Re-check score and iterate; source reached 94 with remaining issues (e.g. needing more images).

Use the app's keyword research tool (keyword ideas, volume, trends) to pick keywords, its 'analyze my keywords' to see what you already rank for, and its competitor tracking to watch which keywords rivals rank for and how they change.
caveats: Scores are app-specific heuristics, not Google rankings; source says 94 was 'good' without claiming rankings.
Source appears to be affiliated with the app (offers a discount code); treat recommendations accordingly.
Paid tiers gate some features; free tier may suffice for small stores.

cards.title: Automate Image Compression Instead of One-by-One Optimization
cards.summary: Use an app's bulk optimizer to compress published product images and collections at once instead of manually processing each image.
cards.use_when: A speed or SEO audit flags uncompressed images on product and collection pages.
steps: Identify uncompressed images via the speed/SEO audit issue list.
In the optimization app, choose to optimize published product images, collections, and similar asset groups.
Trigger a bulk 'optimize all' so images compress in the background rather than exporting each image to a free compressor and re-uploading individually.
Sequence the work: compress images first, then speed up the store, then do on-page SEO — the source presents this as the natural order.
caveats: Only optimize published assets you actually serve; keep originals if you may need higher resolution later.

cards.title: Reclaim Stale Keywords and Add Rich Snippets via an SEO App
cards.summary: Audit what your store already ranks for, fix pages ranking for dead keywords, and toggle on FAQ/product/rich snippets without code.
cards.use_when: Looking to grow organic traffic or improve search result presentation for existing pages and products.
steps: Run the app's 'analyze my keywords' to see the keywords your store already ranks for.
Check whether any pages or blog posts rank for keywords with no search volume or that lead nowhere useful; adjust that content or page to target different, higher-value keywords.
For rich results (FAQ snippets, product grids, top/bottom snippets, side image), use the app's search appearance section and simply turn each snippet type on — no code editing required.
After enabling a snippet, run the app's test to confirm it's correctly added before assuming it will display.
Use the app's broken-link finder to locate dead links (404s) and remove them; use its backlink tracking to build linking authority and support higher rankings.
caveats: Snippet visibility is ultimately controlled by Google and may change; the app test confirms markup, not guaranteed display.

cards.title: Two Root Causes of Slow Shopify Stores: Layout Stability and Apps
cards.summary: Prioritize speed work around CLS/LCP layout stability and third-party app scripts that load with your theme.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing slow mobile load times or deciding where to spend speed-optimization effort on a Shopify store.
steps: Separate issues into two buckets: layout stability (CLS, LCP) and app scripts loading from third-party servers.
Recognize that even simple themes with little customization accumulate speed issues, and the source attributes most of them to apps rather than the theme.
Don't remove apps wholesale — you need them to test and run the store; instead load their scripts later (after user interaction) to reduce their blocking impact.
Frame the goal as loading the theme first and letting app functionality kick in afterward, rather than degrading app use.
caveats: App lazy-loading may break apps that genuinely need to run immediately; verify each app after changing its loading.

cards.title: Find App Scripts Injected via the async Function in Your Theme Head
cards.summary: Locate the async injection function in the store head to see every app script being loaded with your theme.
cards.use_when: Investigating which apps are blocking your Shopify store load or adding layout shift.
steps: Right-click the live store and open Inspect, then expand the head tag.
Scroll for empty/unnamed script tags and open them one by one; the app-injection function ('async' function) is usually in the last one but check all if unsure.
Inside you'll see the links for every app script injected into the theme (e.g. Trustpilot widget scripts) and can see how many scripts each app contributes.
Use this list to judge which apps load at the same time as the theme and are candidates to delay.
caveats: Shopify theme internals and the injection mechanism may change; verify against your current theme.

cards.title: Delay All App Scripts to Human Interaction via content_for_header
cards.summary: Comment out content_for_header and inject a script that defers app loading until the user scrolls, clicks or moves the mouse.
cards.use_when: A simple Shopify theme still scores poorly because many app scripts load during initial render.
steps: In your theme's code editor, find the content_for_header tag — it's responsible for injecting all app scripts.
Comment that tag out.
Paste the lazy-load script (source provides one; you can also write your own delaying the async injection) directly underneath the commented tag and save.
Wait a couple of minutes before retesting speed — testing immediately returns the old score.
Verify: open the console, refresh, and hover/scroll on the page; you should see a confirmation message and the app widgets (e.g. Trustpilot badge) appear only after interaction.
In the source's run, mobile speed moved from roughly 37-38 to 48-50, but significant blocking time from other apps remained.
caveats: Requires editing theme.liquid; back up the theme first.
Apps that must render immediately may not function correctly — test each app after applying.

cards.title: Lazy-Load a Cookie Banner Script to Eliminate Its CLS and Blocking
cards.summary: Comment out a hardcoded cookie-banner script tag and add its URL to a lazy-load function so it appears after user interaction.
cards.use_when: A cookie consent banner loads with the theme and registers layout shift or blocking time in speed tests.
steps: Search theme.liquid for the cookie banner's script tag (the source found one already carrying a defer attribute).
Confirm the banner is creating CLS by checking the layout shift report.
Comment the original script tag out and add the script's URL to the lazy-load function's list, placing that function above the closing head tag.
Save, reload the store: the banner should not appear until the user clicks, scrolls, touches, moves the mouse or presses a key — the function generates the script tag on that interaction.
Verify in the console that the custom interaction message appears on mouse entry. In the source's run, CLS disappeared and mobile speed rose from around 48-50 to 57.
caveats: Delaying a consent banner may have legal/compliance implications depending on your jurisdiction; confirm with your policy requirements.

cards.title: Lazy-Load App-Embed Widgets by Copying Their JS and CSS URLs
cards.summary: Disable an app embed, capture its script and stylesheet URLs from the DOM, and load them through the lazy-load function instead.
cards.use_when: A theme customizer app embed (chat widget, review widget) renders immediately and you can accept loading it after interaction.
steps: In the theme customizer, go to App embeds and confirm which app is injecting (toggling off removes its script, toggling on adds scripts directly to the head rather than via the async function — that's why it loads early).
Leave the toggle on temporarily, refresh the live store, open Elements in devtools and search for the app name (source searched 'vanchat').
Find the app's JS element, right-click > Edit as HTML, copy the script URL, and add it to the lazy-load function's script list (add a comma if appending to an existing entry).
Copy the accompanying CSS URL and paste it into the function's CSS area, then save.
Now toggle the app embed OFF in the customizer and save — the function will inject its files on interaction instead.
Verify the widget appears only after hover/scroll. Source's run: blocking time dropped sharply and the score moved from 57 to around 65, holding above 60 on retest.
caveats: Only do this for apps that don't need to be on screen immediately.
App URLs and DOM structure can change with app updates; re-verify after app upgrades.
Test the app's full functionality after lazy-loading it.

cards.title: Audit theme.liquid for Scripts Missing defer or async
cards.summary: Loop through theme.liquid scripts and add defer (or async) to third-party tags that block rendering.
cards.use_when: Starting a Shopify speed audit or after the major app-script issues are addressed.
steps: Open theme.liquid and scan for script tags lacking a defer or async attribute; Shopify now flags these for you.
For each, identify which app it belongs to (e.g. the source traced a script to an 'ILO Banner' cookie banner) and choose which attribute to apply.
Prefer defer: async loads alongside the page, while defer waits until the site is downloaded and then fetches the script, producing less blocking time.
Add it as either defer or defer="defer" — both work identically.
Test whether the app still functions after adding defer; in the source's case the cookie banner still worked, meaning it didn't truly need to load immediately.
caveats: Some apps break if their scripts are deferred and genuinely require immediate execution.
Expect small gains from this alone — it's a cleanup step, not a headline fix.

cards.title: Retest Speed Three Times and Average to Defeat Caching Lag
cards.summary: Run multiple speed tests after each change and average them, because test servers may serve cached older versions of your store.
cards.use_when: Verifying whether a speed change actually worked, or when results swing wildly between runs.
steps: After making a change, wait a couple of minutes before testing so files propagate.
If you test immediately, the test may evaluate an older cached version and return essentially the same score, making you think your change did nothing.
Run three tests and average the result rather than trusting a single run.
Expect to spend most of your speed-audit time waiting for tests to complete — be patient.
Note that apps loading on the store can make results swing a lot between runs.
caveats: Source-specific practice, not a measured statistical method; use it as a practical heuristic to reduce false negatives.

cards.title: Find Layout Shift Sources by Throttling Network to Slow 3G
cards.summary: Throttle the browser to 3G or a custom slow profile and refresh to watch elements move, identifying what causes CLS.
cards.use_when: Google reports a significant layout shift score but you can't tell what is moving or why.
steps: Open devtools Network tab, set throttling to 3G — the source found 3G still too fast to see movements clearly.
Create a new custom throttling profile at a slower speed (source used ~20 kilobits per second) and refresh.
If it still looks fast, switch to another profile and back to your custom one, then refresh — throttling sometimes doesn't apply directly.
Watch elements populate slowly, then stop the page load when you spot the element in question so you can inspect its state mid-load.
Optionally generate a loading GIF of your store via a third-party capture site to visually spot movement, though the source notes such tools may not register the same CLS that Google does.
caveats: This is a manual diagnostic; you may need several attempts to catch the shift.
A GIF capture tool may not show the same CLS measurement Google reports.

cards.title: Fix Theme-Level Layout Shift Caused by Body and Inline Styles
cards.summary: Remove or reposition inline CSS that rewrites base styles late in the load and causes content to jump.
cards.use_when: A speed test reports a large layout shift, especially a jump involving the header or full page width.
steps: In the theme, check whether the body tag needs style display block — the source had historically added it to the Dawn theme to fix a jump.

Look for inline styles that override base CSS loaded earlier: in the source, a 'page width 70%' style placed in the body tag shrank the page after it initially rendered full width, registering as CLS.

Test removing that style to confirm it's the cause, then place the style sheet at the end of the head tag instead of in the body — the source found this both removed the CLS and loaded faster because the style no longer waited for everything to load.
If the shrink was intentional on desktop, wrap the rule in a media query (source used min-width 767px) so mobile stays full width instead of showing shrunken text and white side bands.
Where possible, use the theme's own layout width settings rather than hardcoded max-width to achieve the desired desktop width.
caveats: Always confirm the intended design before removing styles the client wanted — source kept the 70% desktop width, only scoping it.
Theme file structure differs across themes.

cards.title: Mark the First Visible Item Eager, Keep the Rest Lazy
cards.summary: Fix LCP by forcing the first in-view image (e.g. first carousel/collection card) to load eager while the remaining items stay lazy.
cards.use_when: A lazy-loaded image that is visible on initial mobile view is hurting the LCP in speed tests.
steps: Identify anything visible on first paint — logo, hero banner, and the first slide/card — and check whether it carries loading lazy; visible content should not be lazy-loaded.
In the theme customizer, note the order of sections (source had a slideshow then a collection list) and open the relevant section's liquid code.
In the collection list section's for-loop, assign a variable named lazy: set it false when the for-loop index equals 1 and true otherwise.
Pass that variable into the card snippet by adding a line like lazy: lazy where the snippet is rendered.
In the card collection snippet, replace the hardcoded loading lazy attribute with logic that outputs loading eager when lazy is false (first block) and loading lazy otherwise.
Verify in the DOM that the first card renders loading eager and subsequent cards stay lazy, then retest. In the source's run this pushed mobile speed over 50.
caveats: Only the first in-view items should be eager; making everything eager re-creates the original problem.
Exact section/snippet names vary by theme; adapt the loop variable to your theme's structure.

cards.title: Verify Each Lazy-Loaded App Still Works After Changing Loading
cards.summary: After deferring any app script, test the app's actual functionality, and reverse the change if it breaks.
cards.use_when: Any time you defer, async, or lazy-load an app or theme script on a live store.
steps: After each change, load the storefront and exercise the app: open the chat widget, confirm the review badge renders, check the cookie banner appears on interaction.
Use the console message from the interaction script to confirm scripts were actually injected.
If the app breaks, restore the original script placement or re-enable the app embed — some apps' properties make them break when deferred.
Decide per app whether it truly needs to be on screen immediately or can wait for interaction; only defer the ones that can wait.
Keep a record of what you deferred so future app updates can be re-checked.
caveats: An app may appear to work while a less-visible feature (e.g. form submission, tracking event) is broken; test the full flow, not just rendering.

cards.title: Don't Trust Third-Party Caching Scripts on Shopify
cards.summary: Shopify already caches store files, so a caching service script adds little and can be left alone.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a speed tool or script that claims to speed up a Shopify store via caching.
steps: Identify scripts on your store belonging to unknown speed or caching services.
Test the actual impact by commenting the script out and re-running speed tests; the source found speed remained essentially the same.
Given Shopify handles caching automatically, don't add a caching service expecting gains, and don't remove a script you don't understand unless testing proves it's inert.
If a mystery script's effect is unknown, leave it alone rather than risk breaking storefront behavior.
caveats: Based on the source's informal testing of one such script, not a controlled study.

cards.title: Follow the Speed Work Order: Defer, Lazy-Load Apps, Fix CLS, Fix LCP
cards.summary: Apply speed fixes in the order the source demonstrates: add defer where needed, lazy-load app scripts, resolve layout shift, then correct eager/lazy image loading.
cards.use_when: Working a Shopify mobile speed score up systematically toward and past 50.
steps: Start by adding defer to render-blocking scripts in theme.liquid where apps tolerate it.
Then lazy-load app scripts via the content_for_header override and per-app embed technique.
Then hunt and fix CLS by throttled inspection and correcting offending inline CSS.
Then fix LCP by making first in-view images eager while keeping others lazy.
Retest three times after each stage and average, allowing a couple of minutes for changes to propagate.
Source's documented progression on a real store: about 33 to over 50 mobile; app-script lazy-loading alone was credited with roughly 10-15% improvement when apps were the bottleneck.
Use the outcome as directional — the same sequence won't produce identical numbers on a different store.
caveats: Results are a single-account case study, not a guaranteed benchmark.
If apps aren't your bottleneck, the lazy-load step may be far less effective, as the source itself cautions.

cards.title: LCP diagnosis: the largest-in-viewport element and its delay source
cards.summary: Identify what the largest contentful paint element actually is, then remove whatever mechanism delays its display rather than optimizing unrelated assets.
cards.use_when: Product or landing page speed audit where Google PageSpeed shows a poor LCP score and you need to decide what to fix first.
steps: Run the PageSpeed/Google test on the actual PDP or landing page you send paid traffic to, not the homepage. The source notes that even when the homepage scores fine, the page receiving ad traffic often has a huge LCP problem.

Open Chrome DevTools, go to the Network tab, disable cache and set throttling to fast or slow 3G, then reload. Watch what actually renders. In the reviewed store the layout and secondary images appeared, but the main product image did not — the image file was already downloaded but not shown.

Trace why it isn't shown. In the reviewed example the cause was a slideshow/carousel plugin: its JavaScript had to load before the first big image rendered, so the image sat hidden even after downloading.

Fix the delay at its source: keep the main product image out of the lazy-loaded carousel path, use a plain img that renders immediately, and remove any preloader/placeholder that hides the in-view image.

Add a preload link for that specific image in the head (see the preload card) and consider a more benefit-legible main image, since a confusing main image also hurts comprehension when the shopper lands from an ad.
Re-test three times and average the results to confirm the change is constant rather than a one-off test.
caveats: The source's affected store measured around 5 seconds LCP before and expected roughly 50-60 after a preload fix; treat these as that store's numbers, not benchmarks.
Desktop often already scores acceptably; the source focuses mobile because that is where slow-connection shoppers experience the store.
Editing theme.liquid requires a theme backup or duplicate before publishing.

cards.title: Handling loading="eager" vs "loading="lazy" in collection and card loops
cards.summary: Set the first rendered collection image to eager and everything below to lazy via theme logic, so above-the-fold winners aren't delayed by lazy loading.
cards.use_when: Collection pages, homepage collection lists, or recommendation grids where you render many product images in loops and want above-the-fold images to load immediately.
steps: In the collection-list / grid section, add logic that tracks which card is first in render order. Assign that card's image loading="eager"; assign loading="lazy" to all subsequent cards.
Push the same logic into the product card snippet so individual cards inherit the correct loading attribute rather than relying on a hardcoded value.

Recognize the failure mode being fixed: when every image is lazy (including the first, in-view one), the browser delays the largest visible image; when everything is eager, non-visible images compete for bandwidth.
Verify in the rendered page source that only the first in-view image has loading="eager" and the rest are lazy.
Apply the same rule to hero banners, logos and slideshows — anything in the viewport should never be lazy loaded (see the above-the-fold card).
Re-test the affected page three times and average before/after to confirm the change holds.
caveats: The source reports this change contributed to a jump from 33 to 58 on mobile and desktop moving to 93, but it was one of several changes made together, so the improvement is not attributable to this step alone.
Only the images genuinely in the first viewport should be eager; marking everything eager recreates the original contention problem.

cards.title: Splitting above-the-fold assets from lazy-loaded assets
cards.summary: Lazy loading belongs only below the fold; in-view images, logos, hero banners and slideshows should be preloaded with high fetch priority instead.
cards.use_when: Deciding which images and assets in a theme's header, hero or product gallery should be lazy loaded and which should be preloaded.
steps: Inventory every image/video that renders in the initial viewport: logo, hero banner, main product image, first slider frame, first row of product cards.

For those, do not add loading="lazy". Instead preload them: add link rel="preload" tags in the head listing the URLs of visible images, fonts and critical assets, and set fetch priority as high so the browser treats them as important.
For everything below the fold, keep loading="lazy" on images and add preload="none" on videos so they don't interrupt more important downloads.

Do not display a preloader bar or placeholder in place of an in-view image — the source describes that as an LCP generator because the image is already known to be needed and any delay showing it hurts LCP.
Avoid transition/animation effects that delay in-view elements from appearing.
Confirm the lazy/eager split visually under 3G throttling with cache disabled.
caveats: The source states Google will penalize lazy-loading above-the-fold images — cited as the presenter's guidance rather than a stated numeric rule.
Preload too many assets and you recreate contention; restrict preloads to genuinely in-view, business-critical assets.
LCP and CLS can reappear as the store matures and new sections or apps are added, so this needs periodic re-checking.

cards.title: CLS from images without dimensions: reserve space with width and height
cards.summary: Give image tags explicit width and height attributes so the browser reserves layout space and content below doesn't jump when the image loads.
cards.use_when: Any PDP, homepage or landing page where content shifts as images load — the typical symptom is text pushed down after a hero or inline image appears.
steps: Understand the mechanism: the browser paints background, then text, and only later the images; when an inline image arrives its container expands to full image height and pushes everything below it down. This is one of the main CLS generators.
Add width and height parameters to every image tag so the browser can reserve the correct box before the file arrives.
Reproduce the shift to confirm the fix: open DevTools, Network tab, disable cache, set throttling to slow 3G or fast 3G — on fast Wi-Fi the shift may be too quick to see with the naked eye.
Also run a Lighthouse test and open 'see original trace' to inspect the loading timeline and spot above-the-fold layout shifts.
Treat non-user-initiated movement as the target; if the user clicks and the page then changes, that is not classified as CLS.
Re-verify under the same throttle after the change.
caveats: Setting width/height works only if the CSS respects the aspect ratio; conflicting CSS rules can still override the reserved box.
CLS can also come from app widgets and font swaps, which need separate fixes.

cards.title: Stopping app-widget CLS by reserving the widget container
cards.summary: Reserve fixed width and height for app-injected widgets so their late appearance doesn't push page content down.
cards.use_when: A PDP or homepage uses a review, loyalty or upsell app widget that pops in after load and shifts the content below it.
steps: Identify the app-injecting element in the CLS report: the Google test outlines the shifting element. Copy its CSS classes, open your page, right-click > inspect, use Ctrl/Cmd+F to search the classes and locate the HTML tag.
Diagnose why it moves: app widgets load after the theme's own assets, so their container has no reserved space and the whole page below drops when they render.
Measure or approximate the widget's rendered width/height, then add a CSS rule fixing the width and height of that container so the space exists from first paint.
Alternative diagnose: look for two contradicting CSS rules where one stylesheet sets a height and a later one changes it; remove the redundant rule instead of reserving space.
Test the widget still functions correctly after the CSS change, on a duplicate theme first.
Re-run the speed test and check Search Console > Core Web Vitals to see whether search performance was being affected by the shift.
caveats: Fixing the container size can clip widget content if the widget is responsive or its size varies; verify on the real breakpoints you care about.
The source states CLS issues shown by Google are real, not measurement errors, and that CLS affects search ranking — presenter's position, not a numeric guarantee.

cards.title: Matching fallback font metrics to the custom font to prevent font-swap CLS
cards.summary: Pair font-display: swap with CSS that sizes the fallback font to match the custom font, so text doesn't resize when the swap happens.
cards.use_when: A store uses custom or multiple brand fonts and you see text-size shifts during load, or CLS is attributed to font changes.
steps: Search the theme's CSS files for @font-face rules.
If the rule lacks font-display: swap, add it — this shows a default browser font while the custom font downloads, improving perceived speed.
Account for the side effect: default and custom fonts differ in size and line height, so at swap time the text changes size and shifts the layout.
Add CSS that styles the fallback font to match the custom font's size as closely as possible, effectively reserving the same space the custom font will occupy.
Verify under 3G throttling with cache disabled, since on fast connections the swap may be invisible.
Consider consolidating the number of custom fonts, since the source notes font files slow the site down, especially with multiple fonts used for design flourish.
caveats: Exact matching is hard; the goal is minimizing the shift, not eliminating it.
Swap without metric matching trades a slight delay for a layout shift — decide per font whether the brand font is worth it.

cards.title: Removing residual code from uninstalled apps and old tracking
cards.summary: Hunt leftover app dependencies and dead scripts in theme files, because uninstalling an app does not remove what it installed in your theme.
cards.use_when: Speed cleanup pass on any live theme, especially after removing apps, changing analytics, or when 'remove unused JavaScript' keeps appearing.
steps: Open theme.liquid and look for mentions of apps you have uninstalled (the source's example: a YOTPO script left after removing YOTPO). Remove them.
Check whether a script belongs to an app: go to Apps in admin and confirm whether the app is installed. Some scripts belong to apps listed as sales channels, so check that list too.
If you can't identify a script or app, ask whoever managed the store — it may belong to an external service not listed in Shopify's app store.
Search all theme files, not just theme.liquid, for the script name. The source recommends the 'Shopify theme file search' Chrome extension for this, or a code editor.
Also remove dead tracking pixels, scripts, custom fonts and other assets that no longer serve sales or conversion.
Back up or duplicate the theme before editing so you can publish/revert safely.
caveats: Some dependencies are JavaScript files, CSS files or rendered snippets, not just script tags.
Removing a script that is still needed can silently break app functionality — verify apps on a duplicate theme before publishing.

cards.title: Deferring or lazy-loading app scripts so they don't block core content
cards.summary: Move app scripts out of the critical path with defer/async, or stop their automatic injection and re-inject them on first user interaction when defer/async breaks the app.
cards.use_when: PageSpeed reports unused JavaScript from app scripts and the store's core content should render before app widgets.
steps: Decide whether the app's widget genuinely needs to appear immediately at first paint. The source argues most apps don't; their scripts should be lazily loaded so core content loads first.
If the script is visible in theme.liquid, add defer so it runs only after the document is downloaded. Then verify the app still functions — some apps break with defer.
If defer breaks or the app stops loading, try async, which downloads alongside the document without blocking it. Verify again.
If you can't find the script in theme.liquid, it is being injected automatically. Find the injection point: search for content_for_header in theme.liquid.

Inspect the page head to find the injected inline script and the app's URL inside its async function. Capture content_for_header with Liquid, redefine it with that script removed, and turn the app's admin/customizer toggle off.
Add your own small script that injects the app script on user interaction — click, scroll or other input — then verify app functionality and re-test.
caveats: You must test app functionality after each change; a script that fails to inject may silently remove reviews, upsells or loyalty features from the storefront.
Tracking pixels should not be deferred, per the source, because deferring them can corrupt collected data.
Injecting scripts on interaction can delay widget display until the shopper engages — check whether the widget's value depends on being visible at load (e.g. review stars above the fold).

cards.title: Lazy-loading Shopify's dynamic payment button script
cards.summary: Treat the dynamic payment button script like an app script: disable it if unused, or remove it from content_for_header and re-inject on interaction.
cards.use_when: Cart or PDP speed work where the dynamic checkout / payment button script is heavy and you aren't sure customers use those buttons.
steps: Check whether shoppers actually use the dynamic payment buttons (e.g. Shop Pay / wallet buttons) placed under the add-to-cart button.
If they don't create value, disable the dynamic buttons entirely — the source describes this script as demanding and as slowing the store noticeably.

If you keep them, locate the script to stop it loading: edit theme.liquid and add a line that removes it from content_for_header, using the same capture-and-modify Liquid approach used for app scripts.
Add a case to your human-interaction injection script so the payment script loads when the user clicks, scrolls or otherwise interacts.
Verify the payment buttons still appear and function after interaction on a duplicate theme, then re-test speed.
caveats: Because the buttons appear only after interaction, evaluate whether hiding them until then could reduce wallet-button conversions — this is a trade-off the source does not quantify.
Test on a copy theme before publishing so customers don't see errors.

cards.title: CSS that rewrites base styles from the body tag
cards.summary: Move stylesheets that re-declare base CSS out of the end of the body and into the head, and scope them with a media query when they should only affect desktop.
cards.use_when: A store shows horizontal layout problems or mobile content squished in a narrow column and you're auditing theme CSS load order.
steps: Inspect the DOM and identify any style block or CSS file loading at the end of the body tag that overrides rules already set in the theme's base CSS file.
Understand the side effect: base CSS loads first with basic settings, then the late CSS rewrites them, producing layout problems (the source's case: horizontal issues on mobile).
Move that style into the head, after the base stylesheet, so the cascade is predictable.

If the rule should only apply on desktop, wrap it in a media query so it affects only screens above the relevant breakpoint. In the source's case a media query restricted it to screens over 767px, letting mobile content go full width instead of being squeezed into about 70% width.
Check other symptoms of late-loading CSS: large blank gaps on a PDP are real estate to reclaim, since the source argues the add-to-cart area should sit high on the page.
Re-verify mobile rendering at the widths your shoppers actually use (e.g. an iPhone-class viewport).
caveats: The 767px breakpoint is the source's example, not a universal threshold — pick based on your theme's breakpoints.
Moving CSS can change specificity outcomes elsewhere; check the affected pages, not just the one that prompted the change.

cards.title: Fixing layout shift from the body tag with display:block
cards.summary: Add display:block to the body tag to stop the hero banner rendering low and being pushed up into place.
cards.use_when: A PDP or homepage hero visibly jumps upward as the page loads, or CLS is traced to the initial body/hero rendering.
steps: Reproduce the shift under slow 3G with cache disabled and watch the hero banner area specifically — the source observed the hero loading lower on the page and then being pushed up.
Add display: block to the body tag in the theme's CSS. The source reports this resolved that particular shift.
Combine with width and height on the hero image and any above-the-fold preloads, since body display alone won't fix image-induced shifts.
Re-test with the Google speed test and confirm the CLS element no longer appears in the results.
Run the test multiple times and average to avoid reading a single noisy result.
caveats: This is one specific fix from one store review; if the shift persists, check contradicting CSS heights and app widgets as other causes.
Some themes set body display via their own base CSS — verify your change isn't overridden.

cards.title: Cookie banner modification via a theme property
cards.summary: Address cookie-banner blocking by reconfiguring the banner's property rather than leaving it as a blocking element in the critical path.
cards.use_when: A store's cookie consent banner is identified as a speed blocker during a PageSpeed/theme audit.
steps: Confirm the cookie banner is contributing to blocking or delayed paint in the speed test or DevTools timeline.
In the source's review, the fix was adding a different property to the cookie banner code rather than the mechanism it previously used.
Make changes on a duplicate theme, then re-test three times and compare the average against the pre-change baseline, since the source performed this change alongside several others.
Verify the banner still satisfies whatever consent requirement your store operates under — speed gains do not justify an invalid or missing consent flow.
Re-check both mobile and desktop scores after the change; the source's desktop score, for instance, reached 93 while mobile just cleared 50 in its example.
caveats: The source does not name the specific cookie banner or the exact property value, so treat this as a category of fix to investigate for your banner.
Consent banners are frequently legally required; do not remove or obscure consent to gain speed.

cards.title: The seven-step Shopify speed framework and its order of operations
cards.summary: Work through app reduction, residual code removal, image handling, fonts, script prioritization, CSS deferral and app lazy-loading in that sequence.
cards.use_when: Planning a full speed optimization pass on a Shopify store before or during paid traffic campaigns.
steps: 1. Reduce apps. Every app means fetching assets from another server, and some load their assets as early as possible. If an app doesn't directly boost sales or improve the user experience, remove it, then clean residual code from theme files.
2. Remove residual code: dead scripts, old tracking pixels, unused custom fonts and other assets that don't serve sales or conversion.

3. Fix images: size to the devices shoppers use rather than uploading full-resolution camera files; JPEG under 1MB is the source's stated target for a full-HD-ish image covering any screen; use PNG only when transparency is needed; replace animated GIFs with compressed MP4 video in an HTML video tag; compress images and video (the source names compressjpeg.com as a free option, claiming 50-60%+ size reduction).
4. Fonts: add font-display: swap to @font-face rules and match fallback metrics to avoid CLS.
5. Prioritize scripts: defer non-essential app scripts; async for scripts that should load alongside without blocking; never defer tracking pixels.
6. CSS: defer non-visible CSS with the media onload print technique, but not CSS responsible for in-view elements.
7. Lazy load apps and their assets: load the store's core first, then inject app scripts on click or scroll.
caveats: The listed 50-60% compression figure and the under-1MB JPEG guidance are the source's recommendations, not measured results for your store.
The source ties speed to profitability but provides no conversion benchmark; do not treat speed score gains as guaranteed revenue gains.

cards.title: Choosing app and functionality by value to protect speed
cards.summary: Every app you keep must earn its place in revenue or user experience, because the aggregate script weight compounds as the store matures.
cards.use_when: App audit or cleanup decision on a store that has accumulated apps over time.
steps: List installed apps, sales-channel apps and any external scripts. For each, ask whether it creates real value that translates into more money for the store.
Remove apps whose widget doesn't contribute — the source's framing is that most app widgets do not need to display at first paint.
Check whether remaining apps' scripts can be deferred, made async or injected on interaction (see the app script cards).
Watch for app side effects beyond scripts: widgets that inject HTML and shift layout, and CSS that conflicts with your base styles.

Account for the fact that shops slow down over time: the source describes an initial 60-80% speed score dropping to 40, then to 20, 10 or lower as apps and customization are added — re-audit periodically rather than once.
Check under throttled 3G with cache disabled after each change.
caveats: The source's numbers about score decline are illustrative of typical patterns, not measurements of any specific store.
Some apps genuinely need to render early (e.g. a reviews badge above the fold) — evaluate per app rather than blanket-deferring.

cards.title: Testing protocol: three runs, averaged, on a duplicate theme
cards.summary: Run speed tests three times with gaps between them and average, and make changes on a copy theme before publishing.
cards.use_when: Any speed change you plan to make — establishing a before/after baseline so you don't chase noisy single-test results.
steps: Duplicate the live theme and use its preview link for testing. Note that the source acknowledges the preview link runs slightly slower than the live link, but still shows the difference between states.
Pick a reference page: typically homepage, product page or collection page, depending on where traffic lands.
Run the test three times on that page, allowing some time between runs, and record each result. Without gaps you tend to get the same result.
Average the three results to establish your baseline.
Implement one batch of changes, wait about a minute, then run three more tests and average again.
Compare averages, not single readings, and verify app functionality on the duplicate theme before publishing.
caveats: Preview-link results are inherently a bit slower than live, so compare like-for-like rather than against an absolute target.
The source's example store was described as 'rather basic'; results on heavily customized themes will differ.
Averaging three runs does not remove day-to-day variance in Google's test infrastructure — treat differences of a few points cautiously.

cards.title: Simulating the real shopper's device and connection instead of your desk
cards.summary: Most store owners judge speed on fast Wi-Fi and good hardware; your shoppers are frequently on older phones and slow or patchy mobile connections.
cards.use_when: Before deciding a store is 'fast enough', and when prioritizing which speed work actually matters to paid-traffic conversion.
steps: Test the store the way customers experience it: open it on mobile data away from strong Wi-Fi, or emulate a slow 3G connection in DevTools with cache disabled.

Recognize that a store can look fine on your laptop while a customer on a 3G connection sees a blank or partially loaded layout — the source describes the customer's first impression being a blank page rather than the designed store.
Note the source's stated context: shoppers on older devices and slower networks, and a general claim that many people shopping online use older mobile devices and don't always have fast internet.
Prioritize mobile speed work over desktop; in the source's reviews desktop was often already acceptable while mobile was the problem.
Focus on the page your ads point to — the source observes that ad traffic typically lands on the product page, so that page's LCP and mobile layout matter more than the homepage.
Pay attention to a store scoring around 20% or lower on Google's speed score; the source treats that level as an indicator many customers will struggle or fail to load the store.
caveats: The source references studies about average adult attention span around 8 seconds and claims customers leave after 3-4 seconds of an unloaded layout — these are presented as general claims, not store-specific measurements.
If you don't send traffic to the homepage, the source advises not over-investing there, but still keeping the product-page-to-homepage experience cohesive.

cards.title: Product page mobile layout: get the add-to-cart within the visible band
cards.summary: Use scroll heatmaps to see where shoppers drop off, then compress header and messaging so variants, quantity and the buy button appear far higher on mobile.
cards.use_when: Mobile PDP layout work where the buy button sits below a large header, logo, promo text or gallery.
steps: Pull a scroll heatmap (the source used Hotjar) for the product page. Read the percentages by depth: everyone in the source's example saw the header and first image, then dropped to 93, 91, 80 and so on, with only 20% of visitors reaching the add-to-cart button.
Treat that drop-off as a layout problem: the buy button is effectively invisible to most mobile visitors.

Shrink the mobile logo (the source tried values around 120, 110 and even 100px), reduce or single-line the header text, remove oversized gaps, and keep the mobile layout's horizontal real estate working hard.
Move variants and quantity directly under the reviews, and try placing the benefit row below the buy button rather than above it — the source suggests testing both orders rather than assuming.
Make the add-to-cart button slightly thinner and full page width, and test wording (the source suggests comparing 'add to bag' vs 'add to cart' depending on where your customers are).
Make sure the review badge is present on mobile if it's on desktop; in the reviewed store it was missing on mobile.
