Re-project cost/conversion on a duplicate theme before publishing layout changes.
caveats: The heatmap percentages are from one reviewed store and are an illustration of reading depth drop-off, not a benchmark.
Recommendations such as exact logo pixel size or button thinness are the source's opinions from that review, not universal rules.
Layout changes interact: verify the whole PDP after moving blocks.
Move variants and quantity directly under the reviews, and try placing the benefit row below the buy button rather than above it — the source suggests testing both orders rather than assuming.

cards.title: Clarifying the promo message so shoppers can act on it
cards.summary: Replace multi-variant discount copy with one unambiguous offer so the shopper knows what they're getting.
cards.use_when: PDP or cart promotion messaging, especially sitewide bars or badges combining several incentive types.
steps: Audit the promo copy on the product page. The source flags an example reading '20 to 50% off with free shipping today only'.
Replace it with a single clear offer, e.g. '50% off with free shipping' or '20% off with free shipping'.
Rationale given: people get confused easily, and an unclear offer weakens the page's message and its ability to convert paid traffic.
Check for similar ambiguity elsewhere — separate offer claims in different page sections that appear to contradict each other.
Keep promotion duration and terms consistent with what you can actually honor at checkout; a page promise that checkout can't fulfill creates friction.
caveats: This is the presenter's guidance from a store review, not a tested A/B result.
Discount messaging and margin trade-offs are store-specific; verify the promoted offer is sustainable.

cards.title: Diagnose Shopify's Composite Speed Score
cards.summary: Shopify's admin speed score averages home, collection and product page timings — not a single URL test.
cards.use_when: You need to make sense of the speed score in your Shopify admin versus a single-page Google/Lighthouse test, or you want to know which templates to optimize when improving store speed.
steps: Open the speed score in the Shopify admin and click through to see which pages Shopify says it measures — typically the home page, a collection page and a product page (the most-trafficked ones).
Test those pages yourself multiple times (the source suggests running each 3–4 times and averaging) because a single run varies widely; the Shopify score is essentially an average of the three pages.

Recognize that if you have multiple product or collection templates, fixing only the template Shopify links to gives partial improvement; editing all templates for a page type produces extra speed gain.
After fixing images, scripts or assets, expect a delay before the dashboard score updates — the source's experience is roughly 12–24 hours, driven by store traffic rather than an instant refresh.
Combine the Shopify score with Google PageSpeed Insights and Chrome Lighthouse, since Google surfaces only the top issues and others appear as you fix them.
caveats: Score refresh timing (12–24h) is the presenter's field observation, not a documented SLA; verify against current Shopify reporting.

cards.title: Set a CLS Target and Find Shifts in Lighthouse Trace
cards.summary: Fix layout shift by reserving space for late-loading header, widget and thumbnail elements identified in a Lighthouse 'original trace' inspection.
cards.use_when: Google Search Console flags CLS, a store's organic ranking drops, or you need to find which above-the-fold elements move during page load on your home or product pages.
steps: Run a Lighthouse test in Chrome, then choose 'View Original Trace' and watch the timeline: note the first paint and each point where new elements appear and push existing content down.

In the source's example cases, the culprits were the top menu/header appearing late, the Afterpay widget injecting and pushing content down, and product thumbnails appearing at the bottom — all above the fold.
For an element whose size is contradicted by two CSS rules (e.g. two stylesheets setting different heights), remove one conflicting rule.

For an app that injects a widget (like reviews), determine the container size the widget needs and add CSS reserving that fixed width and height so the rest of the page doesn't move when the widget loads.
Repeat across home, collection and product pages, since each has different apps and scripts loading.
caveats: The source's target: keep CLS under 0.25, ideally near 0.1 or 0; the presenter's case dropped 0.73 → 0.13 → 0.1 → 0 over roughly 28 days, which is an example, not a promise.
CLS data in Search Console lags real fixes by days/weeks.

cards.title: Recompile Critical CSS for Lazy-Loaded Theme CSS
cards.summary: When theme CSS is lazy-loaded, inline correct critical CSS so above-the-fold content is styled from the first paint and does not shift when the full stylesheet arrives.
cards.use_when: Your theme delays loading theme.css (or otherwise renders unstyled content briefly) and Lighthouse shows layout shift in the first second on home, collection or product templates.
steps: Confirm the pattern: theme.css downloads only after the rest of the DOM, so for the first second elements render unstyled and then jump into place when CSS loads — often invisible to the eye but captured by Google's test.
Add inline critical CSS for the visible portion of each template so the page looks correct before theme.css arrives.
In the source's example, the theme already had critical CSS for home, collection and product pages, but it was incomplete/miscompiled — the fix was recompiling a correct critical CSS file.
Compile critical CSS with an online critical-CSS generator: feed the full theme CSS file plus the URL you want critical CSS for.
Create separate critical CSS for visually different templates (e.g. a collection page with a banner vs one without).
Insert the snippet that serves the critical CSS inline in theme.liquid, then test repeatedly with Lighthouse, zooming out to catch below-the-fold shifts too.
For any element still moving (e.g. font-size changes), add a CSS rule reserving its final size so the change no longer displaces neighbors.
caveats: Does not fully fix below-the-fold elements; the source admits Google weighs those less but says fixing them anyway is worthwhile.
Lighthouse shows fewer issues than Google Speed Insights; address Lighthouse first, then move to Google's list.

cards.title: Reserve Space for Widgets That Inject Late
cards.summary: Eliminate layout shift from app widgets (review, Afterpay, etc.) by pinning a fixed container size in CSS for the space the widget will occupy.
cards.use_when: A review app, payment widget or similar injected element visibly jumps into place and pushes other content during your store's load, on home, product or collection pages.
steps: Identify the injected widget by watching the Lighthouse original trace or reloading the page; note exactly which element appears and how far it pushes content.
Determine the size the widget needs (inspect it after it renders, or check the app's documentation) then add a CSS rule fixing its container's width and height.
If two CSS files conflict on the same element's height, remove one of the contradicting rules instead of stacking more overrides.
Re-test with Lighthouse and confirm the shift is gone, both at normal zoom and zoomed out to surface below-the-fold shifts the source admits are lower priority.
Cross-check in Google Speed Insights, which surfaces elements Lighthouse omits, and add CSS rules preventing those from shifting too.
caveats: Ongoing Google Speed Insights may show green while Search Console lags by a couple of days.
Presenter's position: most CLS he sees is a CSS issue or an app widget needing reserved space, but other causes exist.

cards.title: Defer or Lazy-Trigger App Scripts to Shield Core Assets
cards.summary: Move non-visible app scripts out of the initial load, then inject them on user interaction so they no longer block store rendering.
cards.use_when: Speed tests flag unused jQuery/app JavaScript that loads in the first second even though the app's widget is not visible, and you still need the app for later interaction (e.g. reviews, SMS).
steps: Screen every installed app against one question: does it directly impact conversion or user experience? If not, remove it; if yes, check whether it needs to load in the first second at all.
On scripts you control (from theme.liquid), add defer or async so they load after core assets; test the app afterwards, as some break with these properties.

For scripts injected by an app's async function, locate the injected script in the theme's head, copy its URL, modify content_for_header to exclude that URL, and list the modified content_for_header — this stops the automatic injection.
Then create a snippet (e.g. lazy-scripts.liquid) containing vanilla JS that re-creates the script tag with that src, triggered on a click or scroll event; render it from theme.liquid.
Re-run the speed test to confirm the delayed app still fires immediately when the user clicks or scrolls, and that the score improves.
caveats: Scripts with pixels/tracking important for ad campaigns (e.g. Facebook, Google) should stay in the initial load and not be deferred.
Delayed app loading is only safe when the widget is not needed above the fold; verify each app still functions.

cards.title: Assess Whether Each Blocking Script Is Visible or Pixels
cards.summary: Triage blocking JavaScript by asking whether the script needs to run in the first second, and cut or delay the ones that don't.
cards.use_when: Google speed tests flag unused JavaScript / 'reduce unused JavaScript' on your home, collection or product page and you need to decide which scripts to keep, defer or remove.
steps: Read the flagged items: 'unused JavaScript' usually means unused during the test's window, not permanently — decide if each script is needed right away.
Begin with an app inventory: remove apps that add no value, that are purely visual, or that you no longer use; uninstalling still leaves residual script tags you must search out and delete.

For each remaining script, check whether its widget is actually visible at load. The source's example: Yotpo and Recharge widgets exist only on collection/product pages, so they don't need to run on the home page.
Conditionally load app assets only on templates that use their widget; this also removes associated 'reduce unused CSS' warnings for that app.
Keep pixels (Facebook, Google) and measurement tools in the initial load since they must track the user right away; keep Hotjar for interaction measurement.
Investigate duplicate injections — e.g. a Facebook script added both manually in theme.liquid and via an app — and eliminate the duplicate.
caveats: You may not be able to minify app-provided code; instead cut it from pages where it isn't needed.
Some app assets (e.g. ones without compression) are outside your control unless you raise it with the app's support or drop the app.

cards.title: Clean Residual Scripts After Uninstalling Apps
cards.summary: Uninstalling an app leaves its scripts in theme.liquid, head.liquid and footer.liquid — remove each residual tag to reclaim speed.
cards.use_when: You have removed or no longer use an app (or plugin) but its assets may still be loading and slowing your Shopify store.
steps: Open theme.liquid and search for the app's name (the source's example searches for 'yotpo' after uninstalling the Yotpo reviews app) and delete every script tag containing it.
Do the same in head.liquid and footer.liquid, since injected assets may live in any of these theme files.
Also audit scripts and style tags for plugins you stopped using — they often linger and keep loading.
Review the full contents of theme.liquid, head.liquid and footer.liquid and judge each entry's relevance; remove any asset with no current function.
Re-run speed tests to confirm the residual assets are gone and the store loads without them.
caveats: Removing script tags can break an app you are still using — verify the specific app is truly uninstalled or unused first.

cards.title: Right-Size Images and Pick the Correct Format
cards.summary: Shrink product/hero images and choose JPEG/PNG/MP4 by need rather than uploading DSLR originals.
cards.use_when: Speed tests show images are too large for mobile, or your store's pages load slowly because of oversized image assets.
steps: Convert large source images to a full-HD-size JPEG compressed under 1 MB — the source states this is sufficient for any screen size, especially for mobile-majority traffic.
Use PNG only when the image needs a transparent background; avoid animated GIFs (unprofessional and heavy) and instead upload a compressed MP4 using an HTML video tag.
For above-the-fold assets like the first hero or main product image, do not lazy-load them; they should load immediately.
Use preload='none' on videos so they load without blocking other elements.
Apply loading='lazy' to images not initially visible; for a carousel, lazy-load the second, third (etc.) images but not the first.
caveats: 'Under 1 MB JPEG is sufficient for any screen' is the presenter's rule of thumb, not a measurement of your specific catalog.
Lazy-loading the first visible image causes layout issues and hurts speed — the source calls this out as a common mistake.

cards.title: Use lazy-sizes for Bulletproof Image Lazy Loading
cards.summary: Trade the SRC for an empty pixel plus a data-src and lazy-load class, then let lazy-sizes swap in the real image.
cards.use_when: You want stronger lazy loading than the native loading='lazy' attribute gives, e.g. for a slide-out drawer or list of images below the fold.
steps: Install a lazy loading plugin like lazy-sizes on your theme.
On each image to lazy-load, set src to an empty pixel, add data-src with the real image URL, and add the plugin's lazy-load class.
Let lazy-sizes replace the src with the data-src URL once the image is needed, so the DOM downloads without being blocked by image requests.
Verify behavior: in the source's example, the drawer's images show gray placeholders first, then the real files download.
Never apply this to images in the initial viewport (hero, first carousel image, main product image).
caveats: The presenter's opinion is that lazy-sizes does the job slightly better than the native property, but the native property works.
Adding it to an image already visible at load defeats the purpose and creates the very layout issues you're avoiding.

cards.title: Font Loading: Add font-display: swap
cards.summary: Large custom font files block text rendering — font-display: swap lets a default font show immediately.
cards.use_when: Your theme uses multiple custom fonts and speed tests show text-rendering delays or layout shifts caused by font loading.
steps: Locate the @font-face rules in your theme's CSS files.
Add font-display: swap to each @font-face rule that lacks it, so a default font displays while the custom font downloads.
This prevents text from being blocked and reduces perceived load time and shift from font-size changes.
If a font-size change still shifts layout, add a CSS rule reserving the element's final size so neighbors don't move.
caveats: Multiple custom fonts increase asset size; consolidating font files reduces the problem at the source.

cards.title: Defer and Async Scripts to Prioritize Core Assets
cards.summary: Add defer/async to non-critical scripts so hero images and core assets download first.
cards.use_when: You control script tags in theme.liquid and want app/plugin scripts to stop delaying core asset loading.
steps: List the scripts in theme.liquid and ask, for each: does this need to load before or after the site is fully loaded?
For scripts not needed immediately, add the defer attribute so they execute after core assets finish; add async to load them in parallel without blocking, when order doesn't matter.
Common candidates for deferral: app scripts whose widgets aren't above the fold; tracking pixels (e.g. Facebook, Google) are the exception that should stay immediate.
Test after altering each script — the source notes some apps stop working when defer or async is added.
Go a step further (for a developer) by loading the entire store and core assets with no app scripts, then injecting those scripts on a click or scroll event.
caveats: Some apps break with defer/async — verify functionality after each change.
The interaction-triggered injection approach may require a specialist to tailor to your scenario.

cards.title: Delay Non-Visible CSS with media-onload-Print
cards.summary: CSS for elements not visible at load can be applied after the page loads, reducing render-blocking time.
cards.use_when: Large CSS files reference elements below the fold and your store's CSS is blocking rendering.
steps: Identify CSS files that style elements not visible during initial page load.
Apply the media='print' onload='this.media=all' technique so the stylesheet is fetched but only applied to the real view after load.
Keep critical CSS (above-the-fold styles) in place so the visible view stays styled from the first paint.
Re-test the page to confirm the CSS no longer blocks loading and the visible area remains correct.
caveats: Confirm the delayed CSS genuinely styles only below-the-fold elements; misapplying it leaves visible content unstyled.

cards.title: Evaluate Speed-Apps and Optimization Vendors Skeptically
cards.summary: Speed optimization apps are not the answer and some vendors use tricks that help the score but not real users.
cards.use_when: You are considering buying a speed-optimization app or hiring a speed specialist for your Shopify store.
steps: Treat 'speed-up' apps with caution: the source states they only work with returning users, if at all.
When hiring a specialist, verify improvements with your own real-user-timing data, not just a Google score — the audience sees tricks that improve ratings while end-user load stays slow.
Accept that there is no fast, one-action fix; expect a series of small changes across pages and templates.

Prioritize serving what's needed for the current view first rather than loading the whole asset library in the first seconds — the source's restaurant analogy: serve the drink, appetizer, first course rather than cooking the entire menu at once.
Work through fixes template by template: after fixing the main page-type templates, also run and fix secondary product/collection templates.
caveats: The 'returning users only' claim is the presenter's experience, not a measured benchmark.

cards.title: Check Page Vitals Before Trusting Them
cards.summary: Passing vitals (LCP/CLS) does not guarantee a good speed score — validate all three key pages.
cards.use_when: Your home page shows 'all vitals passed' and you're deciding whether store speed is genuinely healthy, or you're auditing a store for the first time.
steps: Run speed tests on all three pages Shopify uses — home, a collection page and a product page — not just the home page.
Do not equate passed vitals with a good score; the source's example store passed vitals yet scored 18 on home, 38 on collection and worse on product, combining to roughly 20.
Aggregate a picture across pages: pages can carry different apps/scripts, so one page may be fine while another is broken.
Fix the main issues (app load, JS blocking, image sizing, CSS), then expect new issues to surface in the test list as old ones are cleared.
Re-run every page type and every unique template repeatedly until the score improves.
caveats: The 18/38/≈20 figures are one audited store's example, not benchmarks for your store.

cards.title: Reproduce the Original Page-Speed Audit Method
cards.summary: A repeatable pass: inventory apps, cut blocking JS, size images, fix CSS, and test home/collection/product pages.
cards.use_when: You're running a full speed audit of your own Shopify store for the first time and need a consistent sequence of steps.
steps: Install no new apps yet; first inventory existing apps and remove any that don't directly affect conversion or UX.
Look at the JavaScript blocking delay (the source's example showed 2.7s from apps) and check for duplicates like Facebook pixel loaded twice (e.g. manual edit plus app).

For each app script, ask whether it needs to load at page load: social widget, PostScript, etc. can often be loaded later or removed if unused. Keep pixels and heatmaps (Facebook, Google, Hotjar) since they must measure right away.
Fix image sizing flagged as too large for mobile, and apply lazy loading to below-the-fold images only — not the first hero, first carousel slide or product image.
Address blocking CSS — separate critical CSS from non-visible stylesheets — and fix any CSS delays from app widgets.
Where app assets lack compression or minification, either contact the app's support or remove the app; then re-test home, collection and product pages.
caveats: Some listed issues (app compression/minification) are outside your control if you keep the app.
The presenter notes more advanced fixes exist beyond this main list.

cards.title: Understand the Three Core Web Vitals and Their Thresholds
cards.summary: The three Core Web Vitals metrics—LCP, FID, CLS—and the specific thresholds you should chase on every product and landing page.
cards.use_when: Setting performance targets for your storefront's key templates (homepage, category, PDP, checkout) before or during a speed optimization project.
steps: Treat LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) as your loading-performance metric: the time until the largest image or text block renders. Target under 2.5 seconds; the source treats anything over 4 seconds as bad and likely to hurt SEO.

Treat FID (First Input Delay) as your interactivity metric: the time from a user's first click to the browser processing that event handler. Target under 100 ms; over 300 ms is bad. The source's framing: you don't want a page that renders while its controls don't work.
Treat CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) as your visual-stability metric: unexpected jumps/movement of elements. Fix it by reserving space so late-loading assets don't shove content around.
Prioritize by element, not by metric: identify the largest above-the-fold element (often a hero image or headline) for LCP, and the elements that jump for CLS.
Note the thresholds are the source's framing of Google's guidance; verify current thresholds against Google's live documentation since these bands can change.
Because customers bounce when a slow page denies them instant gratification, the source argues page-load performance is directly tied to revenue—so don't deprioritize speed behind cosmetic redesigns.
caveats: FID only captures delay on the first input; it says nothing about ongoing responsiveness after first interaction.
The source presents 2.5s/4.0s, 100ms/300ms bands as the practical good/bad lines, not a fine-grained calculation.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Diagnose LCP Bottlenecks with the Network Waterfall
cards.summary: Use the browser Network tab waterfall to find the wide-bar assets delaying Largest Contentful Paint.
cards.use_when: When your homepage, category page, or PDP loads slowly and you need to identify which specific asset is the LCP bottleneck.
steps: Open your store page and open the browser's Network tab, then look at the network waterfall.
Scan for assets drawn as very wide bars; the source says these are your bottlenecks because they take the longest to load.
Identify which asset is actually the largest rendered element (often the hero product image or headline) and check whether it's the one blocking LCP.
Cross-check with the Web Vitals Chrome extension below—the waterfall narrows the timing, the extension names the exact DOM element.
Once identified, attack the bottleneck with the LCP optimization card (compression, CDN, preload, avoid render-blocking JS).
caveats: Waterfall view is browser- and device-environment dependent; what is slow on your connection may differ on mobile networks, which is where most storefront traffic often sits.
The waterfall shows timing, not which element Google considers the LCP candidate—use the extension for that.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Optimize LCP: Compress, Serve via CDN, Unblock Rendering
cards.summary: Four mechanical levers for pulling Largest Contentful Paint under 2.5 seconds on storefront pages.
cards.use_when: After you've identified your LCP element and need concrete fixes for your hero image, category tiles, or above-the-fold content.
steps: Reduce resource load time: compress images and move to modern formats like WebP; reduce fonts to the bare minimum needed to render the page, since each font is a downloaded asset.
Serve assets from a CDN. The source notes deploying to platforms like Firebase or Vercel handles CDN delivery automatically, so you don't manually manage edge caching.

Eliminate render-blocking JavaScript above the fold. If scripts must execute before the hero image displays, they delay LCP. The source cites this as a reason server-side frameworks (e.g., Next.js) beat client-only single-page apps like plain React on initial load—SPAs must run a lot of JS before main content renders.
Use preload links so important assets are discovered first by the browser, and set fetchpriority to high on critical above-the-fold images so low-priority below-fold images don't compete with them.
caveats: Switching rendering architecture (SPA to SSR) is a major rebuild, not a quick tactical fix; only pursue it if the simpler levers are insufficient.
The source's deployment-platform CDN behavior is a snapshot and vendor interfaces change—verify current behavior in your platform's docs.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Make the LCP Element Explicit with Preload and Fetchpriority
cards.summary: Resource-priority hints that ensure the browser fetches your hero content before lower-priority assets.
cards.use_when: When a hero product image or above-the-fold headline loads late because the browser is guessing wrong about priority.
steps: Identify your LCP candidate element first (via the Web Vitals extension), typically the main hero image on a homepage or the primary product image on a PDP.
Add a preload link for that asset so the browser discovers it early rather than waiting on CSS/JS parsing.
Set fetchpriority="high" (per the source's guidance) on the critical image; set low priority on below-the-fold images so they don't load ahead of the hero.
Verify the change reduced LCP in a lab run (Lighthouse or the Web Vitals extension) or field data, rather than assuming the attribute alone fixed it.
Do not over-apply: marking everything high-priority defeats the point and can re-create competition for bandwidth.
caveats: Source states this as a general ability of modern browsers; exact syntax and behavior should be verified against current browser support before shipping.
Preloading too many assets can worsen performance by forcing unnecessary early downloads.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Reduce product-page interaction delay by cutting JavaScript execution
cards.summary: Diagnose and reduce delayed responses to store controls using INP and interaction profiling.
cards.use_when: When customers click add-to-cart, filters, or quantity controls and experience noticeable lag before the page responds.
steps: Measure INP and profile slow variant selectors, filters and add-to-cart controls in current browser performance tools; the source FID extension workflow is historical.
The source says the primary optimization is reducing JavaScript execution time—you cannot simply delete all JS, so move or defer it instead.
Move non-essential third-party scripts (analytics, chat, pixels) off the main thread using Web Workers; the source names Partytown as the tool for offloading third-party scripts to a worker.
Use framework lazy loading (e.g., React lazy) to defer non-critical components until needed, keeping the main thread free at first interaction.
Consider interactivity-focused frameworks like Qwik, which the source describes as using aggressive lazy loading to achieve instant interactivity—relevant if you're rebuilding.
caveats: Third-party scripts (chat widgets, personalization, remarketing pixels) are common in ecommerce and are exactly the scripts worth offloading; test that the offloaded tool still functions.
Framework-level changes are architectural and costly; treat tools like Qwik as rebuild-time options, not drop-in fixes.
FID has been replaced by INP. Offloading requires integration compatibility; do not move every third-party script to a worker automatically. https://web.dev/articles/vitals
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Prevent CLS with Explicit Image Dimensions and aspect-ratio
cards.summary: Reserve layout space for images and embeds so late-loading content doesn't shove your layout and cause accidental taps.
cards.use_when: When category grids, PDP images, or ingredient/spec elements jump as they load, causing mis-taps or a broken-feeling storefront.
steps: Give every image explicit width and height attributes so the browser can reserve its space before the file loads.
Alternatively, use the CSS aspect-ratio property to reserve space without hardcoding exact pixel dimensions—the source highlights this as the flexible way to avoid CLS.
For responsive images that must change aspect ratio by viewport, use the srcset attribute to serve different images under different conditions rather than letting the layout shift.

Audit known CLS generators in ecommerce: injected advertisements, promotional banners that push content down, and over-ambitious entrance animations. Reserve space for ad/banner slots even when empty.
Verify with Lighthouse or the Web Vitals extension, which names the DOM elements causing shift so you can investigate each.
caveats: Explicit dimensions alone don't fix dynamic content such as personalized banners or promo slots—those need reserved containers.
The source treats animations as a contributor to bad CLS when they do too much; temper motion effects near interactive controls.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Use the Web Vitals Chrome Extension to Name the Exact Problem Element
cards.summary: Google's Web Vitals extension logs the specific DOM elements and subpart timings behind poor LCP and CLS in the browser console.
cards.use_when: When Lighthouse gives you a numeric score but you need to know which actual element on your homepage or PDP to fix.
steps: Install the Web Vitals Chrome extension from the Chrome team, then open its settings and enable console logging.
Open your storefront page and open the browser console; you will receive console logs for CLS and LCP as the page loads.
For LCP, the log names exactly which element affects the metric—that's the element to optimize—and it breaks down subparts such as Time to First Byte and element render delay.
For CLS, the log lists the DOM elements causing layout shift; investigate each and apply the aspect-ratio/dimensions fixes.
Click something on the page to receive an FID log, plus additional measurement chances for interactions after the first.
caveats: The source describes the extension as newly released at the time and says it was in personal use for only a couple of days—verify the current interface and available logs.
Lab measurement on your machine won't equal field performance across your real customers' devices and networks.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Run Site-Wide Audits in Parallel with Unlighthouse
cards.summary: One command audits every URL on your domain in parallel, surfacing outlier pages that drag down sitewide performance.
cards.use_when: When your store has hundreds or thousands of URLs (product, category, and content pages) and manual per-page auditing is impossible.
steps: Create a new directory for the audit work.

Run the command `npx unlighthouse --site <url>` with your store's address; the tool runs Google Lighthouse reports on every page in parallel, so hundreds of pages take only a couple of minutes per the source.
Watch the UI, which shows performance in real time as results come in.
Review results to find outlier pages with very poor performance—the source's point is these are pages you would never have known were slow from spot-checking.
Fix outliers and, since Unlighthouse has an SDK, consider integrating it into your continuous integration pipeline so new deploys can't silently regress page performance.
caveats: Site-wide audits can hammer a production server; run against a staging environment or throttle where appropriate.
The exact CLI flags may change over time—verify against the current Unlighthouse documentation before relying on the command.
Parallel lab audits approximate performance; treat scores as triage, confirming important pages with field data.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Use Lighthouse Scores to Triage, Not to Judge Vendors
cards.summary: How to interpret popular-site performance comparisons and avoid cargo-culting someone else's scores.
cards.use_when: When deciding which performance targets are realistic for your store, or when a stakeholder points at a competitor's high score.
steps: Treat audit scores as triage for finding slow pages, not as an absolute judgment of site quality. The source's sample of major sites (Amazon, Google, Reddit, Hub, Astro) averaged around 90, with Astro's framework homepage near perfect—these are examples, not benchmarks you must hit.

Recognize that a complex commerce site can still perform well: the source expected Amazon to do poorly given heavy imagery but found it actually did quite well, while the Web Vitals extension still showed CLS issues on it.
Prioritize the pages that actually drive revenue (homepage, top category pages, top PDPs, cart/checkout entry) rather than chasing a uniform score across every URL.
Pair the aggregate score with element-level diagnosis (Web Vitals extension, network waterfall) so you fix real user-visible problems rather than optimizing for the audit tool.
Set expectations: a perfect score on a marketing site (like the Astro homepage) is not a fair target for an image-heavy catalog.
caveats: Scores vary by device profile, network throttling, and third-party scripts, so comparisons across different setups are not apples-to-apples.
The source only observed these sites briefly in its own tests; do not treat its impressions as durable benchmark data.
cards.source_name: The ultimate guide to web performance.docx

cards.title: Prioritize speed fixes by financial impact and conversion benchmarks
cards.summary: Maps ecommerce speed benchmarks and revenue math to help operators justify and sequence performance work.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest engineering time in site speed, or building a business case for a performance sprint before a peak sales period.
steps: Establish the source's benchmarks as reference points, not guarantees: Google recommends two seconds or less for ecommerce page load; Portent found sites loading within one second converted at roughly 2.5x the rate of sites loading within five seconds; Deloitte reported a 0.1 second speed improvement lifted retail conversions 8.4% and fast-session spend by nearly 10%; the source also cites conversion dropping about 0.3% per additional second and 70% of consumers saying slow loads affect willingness to buy.

Translate speed into your own money using the source's arithmetic: with a $60 average order value and 5,000 daily visitors, the article estimates a one-second delay could cost about $9,000 per day. Recompute with your real AOV and traffic rather than quoting the example.

Note the source's caveat that all speed-testing tools score differently and any single 'page load' figure picks one marker (e.g. time to first byte), so use scores to guide decisions rather than as absolute truth.

Balance speed against the user journey: the article explicitly says you must weigh speed against a UI that optimizes the customer journey, so don't strip elements that drive conversion just to win a score.

Sequence work by likely payoff: images are cited as 50-75% of page weight, so compression and resizing usually offers the largest early gain; then async/defer scripts, app removal, and Liquid deduplication.
If in-house skills are missing, the source suggests engaging a Shopify Plus Partner for theme-level work.
Verify current Core Web Vitals thresholds and tool interfaces before committing to targets, since Google's metrics and dashboards change.
caveats: Conversion and financial figures are cited from third-party studies and vendor examples; they are illustrative, not guarantees for your store.
Some cited statistics appear contradictory (e.g. 'millisecond improvement' vs '0.1 second improvement' at 8.4%), so treat the direction of the effect as the takeaway, not the exact number.
Benchmark numbers should never be treated as a universal rule; measure your own baseline before and after changes.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Use asset_url to force Shopify CDN cache refresh
cards.summary: Explains how Shopify's asset_url filter appends version numbers so the CDN serves updated CSS/JS instead of stale files.
cards.use_when: After editing theme CSS or JavaScript and finding browsers or the CDN still serve an old version of the asset.
steps: Understand the mechanism: Shopify tells its Fastly-powered CDN when assets (images, JS, CSS) change by appending a version number to generated URLs, e.g. ?v=1384022871. That version tells the CDN to pull the correct version.
Use the asset_url filter (e.g. in Liquid: {{ 'theme.css' | asset_url | stylesheet_tag }}) for CSS and JS references so Shopify auto-appends the version number.
Watch out for hardcoded URLs inside your CSS: the article warns that content referenced directly in CSS is static, won't carry Shopify's asset version, and may not update automatically.
Convert CSS syntax to reference assets through the asset_url filter so updates propagate automatically rather than being pinned to stale URLs.
Double-check the Shopify Help Center's current list of URL filters, as filter names and behavior can change with platform updates.
caveats: This applies specifically to Shopify's asset pipeline; other platforms use different cache-busting conventions.
Verify the current Liquid filter documentation, since Shopify's templating APIs can evolve.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Deduplicate Liquid forloops to cut server execution time
cards.summary: Guides Shopify developers to find and remove repeated theme loops that crawl the same collection data multiple times.
cards.use_when: Auditing a Shopify theme's performance or after multiple developers have worked on the same theme and page rendering feels heavy.
steps: Understand what forloop iteration means in Shopify's Liquid: the system loops (crawls or searches) all products in a collection to find a condition, such as a price or a tag.

Accept that loops are sometimes necessary and beneficial, for example outputting images or product variants, and are less costly on collections with few products. The problem is repetition, not loops in principle.

Review theme code to confirm you aren't running Liquid forloops multiple times looking for the same information, a common symptom when several developers work on one theme and duplicate or conflict with each other's code.
Remove the duplicate iterations so the same data isn't fetched repeatedly during a single render.
Where possible, replace heavy loops with a simpler loop such as product.options_with_values, which exposes option data without crawling the whole collection.
Consult current Shopify Liquid documentation before refactoring, since templating language behavior can change.
caveats: Deduplicating loops requires code access and comfort with Liquid; otherwise delegate to a developer or Shopify Plus Partner.
The article does not specify measurable gains from this fix, so treat it as a structural improvement rather than a guaranteed result.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Audit and remove third-party apps slowing your Shopify store
cards.summary: Shows how app scripts enter the theme head via content_for_header and how to decide whether an app's value justifies its speed cost.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a bloated app stack or evaluating whether to install one more app on a Shopify store.
steps: Recognize the mechanism: most script and CSS files for apps installed through Shopify Admin are injected into the <head> of theme.liquid through the {{ content_for_header }} object, and an app must be rendered before other code loads.
Note the source's threshold: if you have more than 20 plugins installed, you likely aren't using them all, yet they still run in the background and can hurt performance.
Enlist a developer to remove unnecessary apps, including forgotten trials.
Re-test after removals using PageSpeed Insights, GTmetrix, or Chrome DevTools' Network tab (reload the page with the tab open) to see the effect.
Before any new install, ask whether the app's added value outweighs the possible load-speed penalty.

Understand the async nuance from Shopify's Jason Bowman: scripts added via the Script Tag API are async-loaded so page load isn't halted, but scripts added directly into the <head> often impact performance immediately. Prefer the API path where available.
caveats: The 20-plugin figure is a heuristic, not a cutoff; an app's weight matters more than its count.
Third-party app code isn't fully under your control, so removing apps may need developer support.
Shopify's app-injection and Script Tag behaviors may change; verify against current documentation.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Unblock HTML parsing with defer and async on script tags
cards.summary: Explains parser-blocking scripts and the specific defer/async fix, with a before-and-after code example.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing slow first render where the browser appears to stall before showing content on a Shopify or any site.
steps: Learn the definition: parser-blocking scripts force the browser to halt HTML parsing until the script is fully downloaded and executed, so nothing else can continue.

Apply the specific fix: add defer or async to the script tag. Example from the source: parser blocking is <script src="jquery.js"></script>; not parser blocking is <script src="jquery.js" defer></script>.
Remember the clarifying principle: JavaScript itself doesn't block the browser, how JavaScript is loaded determines whether it blocks.
After changing attributes, retest to confirm the site still behaves as intended, since defer/async change execution order and timing assumptions.

Use defer when scripts must run in order after parsing; use async when a script is independent and can run whenever it finishes downloading (the article presents both as valid fixes without prescribing which for which case).
Re-run a speed test to verify the parser stall is resolved.
caveats: Changing load behavior can break scripts that depend on execution order; the source explicitly advises checking the site still works.
The article notes that scripts added directly into the <head> still often impact performance even with async handling elsewhere.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Compress and resize images with correct Shopify size parameters
cards.summary: Covers image weight (50-75% of page), lossless compression tools, correct size requests, sprites, and empty image sources.
cards.use_when: Optimizing page weight across product, collection, or landing pages where images dominate load time.
steps: Start with scale awareness: images account for roughly 50-75% of a web page's total weight, and each image creates its own HTTP request, so trimming them is high leverage.
Apply lossless compression with tools like TinyJPG or TinyPNG to cut file size without visible quality loss.
Use Shopify's built-in image size parameters to request the exact size displayed, which reduces the file downloaded from the CDN and cuts browser-side scaling work.
Hunt for empty image sources such as , which still send an extra request to your servers; remove them.
Consolidate small UI images (icons) into CSS sprites to limit individual image requests.
For assets that shouldn't render immediately, defer them with lazy loading or srcset as a catch-all (the article pairs this with hero-slider guidance).

Set a review habit for stores publishing many products or blog posts, since images tend to be added without scrutiny over time; the source cites a client case where optimization cut image space by 60%.
caveats: The 60% reduction is one agency's client example, not a benchmark.
Shopify's image size parameter syntax should be verified against current documentation.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Replace standard YouTube embeds with lite embeds
cards.summary: Explains why standard video iframes bloat pages and how lite embeds cut nearly a megabyte by loading the player on click.
cards.use_when: A product page, landing page, or homepage uses YouTube or similar video embeds and load time is a concern.
steps: Identify the problem: standard YouTube embed code downloads files even before a visitor clicks play and uses a fixed-size <iframe> that doesn't adapt to different screen sizes.
Adopt lite embeds: on initial page load, only the thumbnail image is embedded; the video player and its JavaScript load when the user clicks inside the thumbnail.
Use the size comparison as motivation: YouTube thumbnails are about 15 kilobytes, so lite embeds can reduce page weight by almost a megabyte compared with a full embed.

Apply the mobile-specific rule: disable mobile video autoplay, because weak cellular connections must then download a large file; replace autoplay with a static thumbnail and a button that triggers the video.
Verify the lite-embed library or approach still functions with current YouTube embedding policy, as embed APIs change.
caveats: Lite embeds trade a tiny bit of click friction for large weight savings; test that the click-to-play experience still converts as intended.
Implementation specifics vary by platform and embed library.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Remove or defer Quick View pop-ups on collection pages
cards.summary: Details how Quick View can pre-load full product page data for dozens of thumbnails and how to detect or replace it.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a Shopify collection or category page that feels slow or bounce-prone, especially on mobile.
steps: Understand the cost: Quick View implementations (theme-built or app-based) sometimes pre-load entire product page data in case a visitor clicks the button. On a collection with 20-30 thumbnails, that's an enormous amount of data loaded up front.
Weigh the customer experience downsides the source lists: Quick View adds an extra step to the journey, can be clicked by accident, and can be mistaken for a product page.
Check whether shoppers even use it using click mapping tools such as Hindsight or Hotjar to see where users scroll and click.
Locate the feature: check the theme customizer for an enable/disable option; if absent, check whether an app provides it; if neither, it's likely baked into the theme and needs a developer.

The source's clear preference is removal. If it must stay, either use AJAX to fetch product information only on click, or store a limited set of product data as data attributes on the grid item and build the pop-up dynamically with JavaScript.
Note the source's own qualification: both alternatives are less ideal than removing it, because product information still loads per product, though less than downloading all images and links.
caveats: The article states even AJAX or data-attribute approaches are inferior to removing Quick View.
Theme-level removal may require a Shopify Plus Service Partner.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Cut pop-ups and hero sliders that add page weight
cards.summary: Sets parameters for pop-up timing and slider count so experiential elements don't sabotage load speed.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a homepage or landing page where promo pop-ups and rotating hero carousels are slowing load.
steps: Set pop-up triggers that don't compete with initial page load: the source recommends displaying pop-ups immediately on load, or using exit-intent or time-delay triggers, so there's breathing room between page load and pop-up load. Too many flashing graphics hurt speed and distract from the content you optimized.
Reduce or eliminate homepage hero sliders: the size and quality needed for a slider to look good increases load times, especially with four to five slides.

Prefer a single high-quality hero image with a clear call to action; the source cites that the brain processes visual imagery about 60,000 times faster than text (attribution: source, not a conversion benchmark).

If a slider is required, follow the article's UX rules: two to three slides maximum, render slides as static content sections rather than auto-rotating carousels, and use srcset or Lazy Load. It points to Chubbies using optimized images instead of a hero slider.

Which one should you start with? Test whether a simplified theme alone helps: the source cites an agency's observation of greater than 50% improvement in homepage bounce rate for new visitors after switching to a streamlined theme, which is an example, not a promise.
caveats: The 94%-design and 60,000x image-processing figures are cited research/opinion in the source; use them as persuasion, not measured KPIs.
The 50% bounce-rate improvement is one practitioner's observation with no stated controls.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Clean up redirects, broken links, and use 301s correctly
cards.summary: Covers how redirect chains and broken assets add HTTP requests and how to consolidate them on Shopify.
cards.use_when: Doing a technical SEO or speed audit of store navigation, collection URLs, or after replatforming or renaming products.
steps: Recognize the cost: too many redirects and broken links hurt performance and SEO rankings; 302 redirects (temporary moves) can hurt SEO and trigger additional HTTP requests and data transfer delays.
Prefer cacheable redirects or Shopify's built-in redirects function within the Navigation panel, which are 301s by default.
Follow the source's rule: never redirect URLs to pages that are themselves redirects, as this creates chains.
Find and remove broken links for page elements like images, CSS, and JS files, which add HTTP requests and sting site speed; use a tool such as Broken Link Checker.

Create custom 404 pages to help visitors who land on an incorrect URL; the source cites Gymshark directing 404s to its two biggest categories, demonstrating a merchandising recovery path from a broken link.
caveats: Redirect cleanup is ongoing, not one-time, especially as products and collections are renamed.
Shopify's built-in redirect behavior should be verified in current admin documentation.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Apply lazy loading to below-fold content
cards.summary: Explains how lazy loading defers off-screen content until visible, with a concrete example of its effect.
cards.use_when: Optimizing a product page, collection, or homepage that loads many images, reviews, or carousels up front.
steps: Understand the principle: lazy loading prevents all content from loading immediately; content only loads when users hit certain triggers.

Apply it to product pages by letting above-the-fold content (title, imagery, description) load immediately while supporting content loads on scroll. User-generated content, social carousels, and customer reviews are cited explicitly as good lazy-load candidates.

Remember the browser behavior this solves: a browser will simultaneously download every image on a page regardless of visibility; lazy load only downloads an image when it can be viewed in the browser.
Use the cited agency example as an illustration of the pattern, not a promise: a client site with a staggering number of below-fold images was improved by lazy loading.
In Shopify specifically, the source also recommends srcset or Lazy Load as a catch-all with hero/slider imagery.
Verify interaction with above-the-fold content so first meaningful paint isn't harmed.
caveats: The source does not quantify conversion impact from lazy loading; it describes the mechanism and one practitioner's experience.
Implementing it incorrectly can hide content from crawlers or delay content users expect immediately.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Consolidate tracking tags with a tag management system
cards.summary: Explains using Google Tag Manager to reduce many tracking JavaScript requests into one, as a speed measure.
cards.use_when: A store loads multiple analytics, conversion, and retargeting tags and page speed is suffering, or you need to disable a failing tag quickly.
steps: Identify the culprit: JavaScript tracking tags for general analytics, conversions, goals, and behavioral retargeting are often to blame for slow performance.
Use a tag manager to organize deployment, triggers and removal of tracking tags. Audit the requests and execution cost of each tag; one container does not make all vendor tags one network request.
Note the operational benefit: if a tag failure takes your site down, a TMS lets you remove the tag quickly.

Use the source's practitioner evidence as direction, not guarantee: Anatta's Nirav Sheth says that when optimizing a beauty client's speed, nothing moved the needle more than combining Shopify API leverage with cleaning up Google Tag Manager.
Standard GTM container setup mechanics are outside this card's scope; follow the Shopify Plus Help Center guidelines for platform-specific configuration.
Re-verify current GTM and Shopify integration interfaces before changing tag setup, as they change over time.
caveats: The GTM 'needle mover' claim is a practitioner opinion from one agency's client project, not a controlled result.
Poorly governed GTM containers can themselves accumulate tag bloat, so the consolidation only helps if it's maintained.
Editorial correction: container consolidation alone does not establish a speed improvement. Measure the resulting store waterfall. https://developers.google.com/tag-platform/tag-manager/web
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Run and interpret website speed tests with the right expectations
cards.summary: Explains PageSpeed Insights, GTmetrix, and Pingdom differences and how to read Core Web Vitals metrics.
cards.use_when: Establishing a speed baseline before optimization work, or verifying the impact of changes.
steps: Accept that each tool scores differently and any 'page load' timing picks one specific marker, such as time to first byte, so scores aren't directly comparable between tools.

Use Google PageSpeed Insights for personalized recommendations and to identify elements like CSS and JavaScript slowing the page; it also scores Core Web Vitals as Good, Needs Improvement, or Poor. Note that on sites meeting Core Web Vitals thresholds, users were cited as 24% less likely to abandon mid-load.

Use GTmetrix for an A-to-F grade merging YSlow and PageSpeed data, including page load speed, Web Vitals/Lighthouse analysis, optimization opportunities, and page composition by requests and total byte size.
Use Pingdom for a 0-100 score and a waterfall analysis that helps identify problem areas line by line; it surfaces recommendations like reducing DNS lookups, fewer HTTP requests, and compression.
Know the core metrics: fully loaded page, time to first byte, and first meaningful paint.
You can also run tests on competitors' mobile sites to see what's wrong with theirs and avoid the same mistakes.
Use results to guide decision-making but keep an open mind; balance speed against a UI that optimizes the customer journey.
caveats: The 24% abandonment figure is cited from research and applies to sites meeting Core Web Vitals thresholds; it is not a universal prediction.
These tools are third-party surfaces and their scoring methodology can change; verify current behavior before using scores as KPIs.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Optimize mobile checkout with Shop Pay and mobile-first speed
cards.summary: Argues checkout is often overlooked in speed work and cites Shop Pay's higher mobile checkout-to-order rate.
cards.use_when: Improving mobile conversion on the path from cart to order, where shoppers abandon due to checkout delays.
steps: Include checkout in every speed optimization effort: the source notes checkout is often forgotten while home, product, and category pages get attention, and failing to optimize it likely raises cart abandonment.
Prioritize impulse shoppers: the article's reasoning is that people are confident enough to select items, but delays at checkout mean they have to really love the product to stick around.

Enable Shop Pay for one-click mobile checkout. The source cites Shopify's figure that merchants using Shop Pay checkouts have a 1.91x higher mobile checkout-to-order rate than regular checkout. Note this is a platform-reported comparison and may involve differences in shopper mix.

Support the pattern with Kotn's stated rationale: most customers discover products on mobile and if they have to fill out a form, they're lost; Shop Pay's million-merchant network even lets new customers check out in one click.
Combine with other mobile speed fixes the source lists: disabling video autoplay, and considering AMP via a Shopify app (AMP, Fire AMP, or The AMP App) if you need it.
Review current Shopify checkout documentation, since Shop Pay availability and third-party checkout rules vary by plan and region.
caveats: The 1.91x checkout-to-order comparison is Shopify-reported and not a controlled independent study.
AMP benefits cited (2x time on page, 20% conversion increase) come from the source and may not transfer; AMP app availability on Shopify should be verified.
Checkout extensibility rules differ by Shopify plan.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Research hosting and platform capacity for peak traffic events
cards.summary: Frames platform/hosting scale as a precondition for speed work, with questions to ask before BFCM-style spikes.
cards.use_when: Preparing a store for a major sales event or choosing an ecommerce platform/hosting plan.
steps: Accept the source's precondition: if your commerce platform isn't committed to making speed a priority, the other optimizations make a smaller difference.

When researching hosting requirements, check for memory or bandwidth limits for scaling during seasonal promotions, and estimate projected traffic and peak user load to avoid crashes from sudden spikes.
Before any major sales event, ask your commerce platform provider to help you prepare for unexpected traffic spikes or an influx of orders.

Weigh the source's evidence: one survey cited 81% of respondents saying 60 minutes of downtime costs their business more than $300,000 (a survey figure, not a guarantee); JB Hi-Fi's site went down two hours during BFCM, illustrating brand damage from outages.

Consider rendering architecture as part of the picture: Shopify's Storefront Renderer (SFR) is cited as 2.5-5x faster for server-side requests, with the biggest gains on cache misses; Rhone Apparel reported a 15% revenue increase, 17% conversion increase, 12% lower average page load, 37.95% lower average server response time, and 3% lower bounce rate after adopting SFR. Treat these as vendor case-study figures.
caveats: All figures here are vendor or survey-sourced case studies published by Shopify, not independent measurements.
Headless commerce and other architectural changes are out of this card's scope and may add complexity rather than remove it.
cards.source_name: Website Speed Optimization Tips for Shopify Stores.docx

cards.title: Measure Perceived Performance With Slow-4G Throttling
cards.summary: Test real-user loading experience in Chrome DevTools by throttling to slow 4G or 3G with cache disabled, rather than chasing a perfect PageSpeed score.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether your product or landing page actually loads acceptably for real shoppers before or after a speed optimization pass.
steps: Open Chrome DevTools and go to the Network tab.
Set the throttling dropdown from 'No throttling' to 'Slow 4G' or '3G' — pick the one closest to your typical visitor's connection (the presenter uses Slow 4G).
Check 'Disable Cache' so you don't fetch assets from memory and mask the real experience.
Reload the page and watch: note time-to-first-content, layout jumps, and slow image reveal in chunks.
Compare against a non-optimized copy of the same page to isolate the impact of your changes.
Remember the presenter's point: third-party scores (PageSpeed Insights, GTmetrix, Gift of Speed) are not the best measure — perceived experience on slow connections is the primary metric.
caveats: Disabled cache is a worst case; most real users benefit from cached assets, so also test with cache enabled to see the typical case.
Presenter's opinion that scores are not the best way is source-specific; scores still correlate with real gains from fundamental fixes.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Set loading=eager Above the Fold and lazy Below
cards.summary: Control image loading priority with the loading attribute so above-fold hero/logo images load immediately while below-fold images defer.
cards.use_when: Optimizing image loading order on a homepage, PDP hero, or landing page where above-fold images must appear fast and off-screen images shouldn't block.
steps: Identify which images are visible on first paint: hero image, logo, above-fold banners.
Set loading="eager" on those — even though it is the browser default, set it explicitly so a later optimization plugin doesn't accidentally lazy-load them.
Set loading="lazy" on all images below the fold, including any repeated logo in the footer.
Note you cannot lazy-load CSS background images with the loading attribute; optimize those files instead.

In Oxygen, add the attribute under the element's Settings/Properties panel (attribute name 'loading', value 'eager' or 'lazy'), and use right-click 'Copy settings' / 'Paste settings' to apply across many images quickly.
After pasting settings, re-add alt text you may have overwritten — decorative images get an empty alt attribute.
caveats: Verify your builder's exact attribute panel, interface labels may differ by tool or version.
Background images are not covered by the loading attribute.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Fix CLS With Explicit Width and Height Attributes
cards.summary: Eliminate cumulative layout shift by hardcoding width and height attributes matching the exact rendered size so the browser reserves layout space.
cards.use_when: Fixing a red CLS score or content jumping on load on your homepage, PDP, or landing page.
steps: On the live front end, right-click the image and choose Inspect.
Find the image tag and hover over the src (source URL) to read the rendered size — e.g. 398x597 px.
In your builder, add a width attribute equal to the rendered width (no 'px' unit) and a height attribute equal to the rendered height.
Repeat for every image; for non-absolutely-positioned images this matters most, but add to absolutely-positioned images as good practice too.
Reuse settings via copy/paste for image sets that share identical rendered dimensions.
Retest in PageSpeed Insights to confirm CLS moves into the green.
caveats: Explicit dimensions reserve space but do not by themselves fix other shift sources (ads, injected content, web fonts).
Presenter's example dropped CLS into the green after two simple changes — a case result, not a guarantee.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Convert and Resize Images With AVIF at 2x Rendered Size
cards.summary: Shrink image files by converting to AVIF and resizing intrinsic dimensions down to 2x the rendered size, keeping retina sharpness at a fraction of the file weight.
cards.use_when: Reducing image payload on image-heavy pages such as homepage heroes, product galleries, or landing pages.
steps: Inspect an image and hover the source URL to read both rendered size and intrinsic size plus current file size (e.g. rendered 398x597, intrinsic 1770x2560, 161KB).
If intrinsic is far larger than rendered, there is waste to remove.
Open the image in Photopea (free, browser-based, no login needed) or an equivalent editor.
Export as AVIF (better compression than WebP/JPG/PNG while retaining quality and supporting transparency); WebP is an acceptable alternative with broad support.
Resize to 2x the rendered size — e.g. 796x1194 for a 398x597 render — so high-density retina screens stay sharp without loading oversized originals.
Keep the export quality slider around 50% (presenter finds the difference imperceptible) and confirm the file size drop.
For background images that must cover a section, keep dimensions but still convert to AVIF.
Swap optimized files into the page and add alt text to each while you work.
caveats: Manual conversion is time-consuming; paid plugins like ShortPixel or Imagify can automate it.
You can also resize via the WordPress media library, but that alone won't give the AVIF/WebP file-size savings.
Presenter's 161KB→~10KB drop is a case example, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Audit Loaded Assets With a Waterfall Chart
cards.summary: Find unnecessary JavaScript and CSS by reading a request waterfall to spot scripts (jQuery, unused WooCommerce files) loaded on pages that don't need them.
cards.use_when: Reducing render-blocking resources on a landing page or homepage before deeper optimization.
steps: In PageSpeed Insights, check the 'Render-blocking requests' section for its flagged items.
For full detail, use the GTmetrix waterfall chart to see every request in load order.
Scan for things you don't use on this page: jQuery (not needed by logged-out users), WooCommerce CSS/JS on a page with no cart or add-to-cart, unused block styles.
Note which assets are global (needed everywhere) versus page-specific (can be unloaded here).
Build a list of assets to remove, then unload them via theme/builder performance settings or a page-level plugin.
caveats: PageSpeed Insights flags may not show every loaded asset; the waterfall gives the complete picture.
Be conservative: unload only what this page truly doesn't use.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Dequeue jQuery for Logged-Out Front-End Users
cards.summary: Remove jQuery bloat from public pages by dequeuing and deregistering it only for logged-out users on the front end, keeping it for admin.
cards.use_when: Trimming render-blocking scripts on public pages where jQuery is confirmed unused but WordPress loads it by default.
steps: Confirm via the waterfall that jQuery (and jQuery Migrate) is loading on your public page.
Create a code snippet (e.g. with WP Codebox) that hooks wp_enqueue_scripts and dequeues plus deregisters jQuery for the relevant scope.
Add conditions so the snippet runs only when needed: front end (location) AND user not logged in — the WordPress admin bar needs jQuery for logged-in users.
Enable the snippet and re-run the waterfall to confirm jQuery no longer loads for logged-out visitors.
Only do this if your theme/plugins truly don't depend on jQuery on the front end, or you'll break scripts.
caveats: Verify current hook and function names against WordPress docs, APIs change.
Tool set (WP Codebox) and snippet UI may differ; confirm the current interface.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Unload Unused WooCommerce Assets Per Page With Asset CleanUp
cards.summary: Surgically remove unused WooCommerce CSS/JS (and other plugin assets) from pages that don't use them, while leaving them active where they are needed.
cards.use_when: A landing page or content page loads WooCommerce or other plugin assets it never uses, slowing first paint.
steps: Install the free Asset CleanUp plugin from the WordPress repository.
Open the specific page in the editor; Asset CleanUp adds a metabox listing loaded files by source (e.g. WooCommerce category with 13 files).
Expand the group and unload files not needed on this page: brand styles, source buster, add-to-cart, block styles CSS, jQuery block UI, etc.
Review each before unloading — the presenter keeps a small 'coming soon' CSS file because its size is negligible.
Save; the unloading applies only to that page, keeping assets elsewhere.
Record what you unloaded — if you later add a WooCommerce feature like a mini cart to this page, you must re-enable those assets.
caveats: Per-page unloading is page-specific; a new page with the same template needs its own setup.
Verify plugin name and interface from current WordPress repo listing.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Unload Default WordPress Bloat for Logged-Out Users
cards.summary: Disable unused WordPress defaults such as emojis, Gutenberg block CSS, dashicons for guests, and pingbacks through builder/theme performance settings.
cards.use_when: Establishing a fast baseline on any WordPress storefront before page-specific fixes.
steps: Open your theme or builder's performance settings (e.g. Oxygen → Performance).
Enable options that fit your site: disable Gutenberg block CSS (if not using Gutenberg), disable emojis, disable dashicons for logged-out users, remove/disable pingbacks.
Skip any option tied to a feature you actually use — if you use Gutenberg blocks, keep block CSS.
Save and re-check the waterfall to confirm the bloat is gone.
Apply site-wide, since these defaults load everywhere.
caveats: Settings locations differ by builder/theme; confirm current UI.
Disabling a feature you rely on can break rendering — audit before enabling each toggle.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Self-Host Google Fonts as WOFF2 to Cut External Requests
cards.summary: Download Google Fonts, convert to WOFF2, and serve them locally to remove the external font-request dependency.
cards.use_when: Reducing third-party font requests and render-blocking on your storefront, especially where fonts are used site-wide.
steps: Find your fonts on fonts.google.com and add them to your list (e.g. Inter, Libre Baskerville).
Download the font files — you get TTF, which you must convert to WOFF2 web-font format.
Convert using Google Web Fonts Helper (recommended; Font Squirrel's Webfont Generator also works but the presenter found it failed on some fonts, possibly variable ones).
In your builder/theme, upload the WOFF2 files as custom fonts, specifying the font weight (e.g. 900) and style (italic/normal) for each.
Name the local versions distinctly (e.g. 'Inter Local') so you can tell them apart in the font picker.
Switch your font variables (body/heading) to the local versions; with variables, one change updates all usages.
If your theme/builder has no custom-font upload, use a custom-font plugin from the WordPress repository.
Re-run the waterfall to confirm Google font requests are gone.
caveats: Conversion tool behavior varies by font; test variable fonts specifically.
Exact custom-font UI differs by theme/builder — verify.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Verify Caching and Compression via Response Headers
cards.summary: Confirm gzip compression and server caching are actually active by inspecting response headers in the Chrome Network tab.
cards.use_when: Checking whether your host's caching and compression are enabled, or verifying after you turn them on.
steps: Open DevTools, go to the Network tab, and enable 'Preserve log'.
Reload the page (no throttling needed) and select the first/primary document request.
Inspect the response headers.
For caching enabled, look for a cache-related header such as x-cache: hit (not cache-control, which may say no-cache, must-revalidate).
For compression enabled, look for content-encoding: gzip (or whatever encoding method your host uses).
To re-verify caching/compression after enabling them, test in an incognito window with 'Disable cache' unchecked so you don't read from browser memory.
caveats: Header names depend on the host/cache stack; x-cache is an example, not universal.
Presenter calls caching/compression a band-aid if fundamentals aren't fixed first — do the content and asset work before relying on them.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Sequence WordPress Speed Work: Fundamentals Before Caching
cards.summary: Fix images, asset loading, and fonts before enabling compression, caching, or a CDN, since infrastructure alone won't fix heavy resources.
cards.use_when: Planning a speed project for a storefront or landing page and deciding what to prioritize.
steps: Start with image loading attributes: eager above the fold, lazy below.
Add explicit width/height to above-fold images to kill CLS.
Optimize and resize image files with AVIF or WebP.
Unload unnecessary scripts/styles on the page, including jQuery if unused.
Remove unneeded WordPress bloat (emojis, Gutenberg block CSS, etc.).
Self-host Google Fonts as WOFF2.
Only then enable caching and compression, and optionally add a CDN as a bonus.
Re-test perceived performance on slow 4G after each stage so you can attribute improvements.
caveats: Presenter states these fixes delivered strong gains with no compression, caching, or CDN enabled — a demonstrated case, not a promise for every site.
'Your mileage may vary depending on your site builder and hosting' — the source explicitly says this.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Interpret Waffling Speed Test Scores and Average Runs
cards.summary: Trust scores only after repeated runs, since tools like PageSpeed Insights fluctuate, and cross-check against perceived performance.
cards.use_when: Compiling speed data for a decision or report and deciding whether your score is trustworthy.
steps: Run the same test multiple times; scores can move up or down between runs even without changes.
Average the results when gathering data for a report or comparison.
Cross-reference across tools (PageSpeed Insights, GTmetrix, Gift of Speed) rather than relying on one.
Weight real-user perceived experience (slow-4G DevTools test) above any single score.
Expect lab tools to re-test in different conditions, so a single lower score after a change isn't necessarily a regression.
caveats: Presenter notes scores are not the best performance measure; this is a source opinion.
Tool interfaces and scoring change over time — verify current behavior.
cards.source_name: WordPress Speed Optimization_ Improve Your Website Performance & Make It Faster (Step-By-Step).docx

cards.title: Apply the WordPress Speed Optimization Checklist
cards.summary: A portable checklist covering image loading, dimensions, file format, asset unloading, local fonts, and caching/compression.
cards.use_when: Running a structured speed pass on any WordPress storefront or landing page.
steps: Set below-fold images to lazy loading and ensure above-fold images are not lazy loaded.
Add fixed width and height to above-fold images to eliminate CLS.
Optimize and resize images, converting to AVIF or another modern format like WebP.
Unload unnecessary scripts and styles on the page, including jQuery if not needed.
Remove as much unneeded WordPress bloat (emojis, Gutenberg block CSS) as possible.
Load Google Fonts locally.
Ensure caching and compression are enabled.
Optionally add a CDN for further speed.
Re-test with slow-4G throttling and cache disabled to confirm the perceived-experience gain.

cards.title: Compare Optimized vs Unoptimized Page Under Throttling
cards.summary: Reproduce the genuine before/after by loading an optimized page and a non-optimized copy in an incognito window on slow 4G with cache disabled.
cards.use_when: Validating that a speed optimization effort actually changed the real loading experience, not just a lab score.
steps: Open an incognito window (so memory cache doesn't hide the effect) and set throttling to slow 4G.
Load the unoptimized version first and note layout shifts and slow image reveal.
Load the optimized version and compare how quickly content becomes usable and whether layout is stable.
Note that global changes (local fonts, removing bloat) carry over to the non-optimized copy, so the comparison isolates page-specific work.
Then uncheck 'Disable cache' and reload to see the more typical cached experience, which the presenter finds near-instant.
caveats: Global optimizations persist across pages and can blur the before/after comparison.
Cache-disabled testing is a worst case, not typical visitor experience.

cards.title: Do Not Lazy-Load Background Images; Optimize Them Instead
cards.summary: CSS background images can't use the loading attribute, so shrink their files with modern formats instead of deferring them.
cards.use_when: Tuning a hero or section background image that must cover an area but is slowing the page.
steps: Recognize that the loading="lazy"/"eager" attribute only applies to elements, not CSS background images.
For background images that must cover a section, keep their large dimensions (do not shrink the intrinsic size).
Still convert them to AVIF (or WebP) to gain file-size savings while retaining coverage.
If measuring CLS, absolutely-positioned background images generally do not contribute, but the presenter still adds width/height as good practice.
Re-test to confirm the background image no longer dominates load time.
caveats: Background coverage constraints limit how much you can resize; format conversion is the main lever.
Verify your builder exposes the format/lazy controls you need.

cards.title: Resize Images to 2x Rendered Size for Retina
cards.summary: Match intrinsic image dimensions to 2x the rendered size so retina screens stay sharp without loading oversized originals.
cards.use_when: Selecting export dimensions when optimizing product photos, hero images, or gallery images for a storefront.
steps: Read the image's rendered size in DevTools (hover the source URL), e.g. 398x597 px.
Multiply both dimensions by 2 to get the export target, e.g. 796x1194 px.
Export at that size in AVIF, keeping the aspect ratio (editors auto-adjust height when you set width).
Do not export at the raw rendered size — retina/high-density screens would look soft.
Do not keep the original oversized intrinsic dimensions — that wastes bytes for no visible gain.
caveats: Presenter's 2x rule is a practical heuristic, not a formal standard; higher-density displays may still benefit from more.
Does not apply to background images that must cover a section.

cards.title: Add Alt Text and Preserve It When Copying Image Settings
cards.summary: Use the image optimization pass to add alt text to every image, and remember copy/paste of element settings can overwrite existing alt text.
cards.use_when: Standardizing image accessibility and SEO metadata while optimizing page images.
steps: While swapping in optimized images, add descriptive alt text for every meaningful image.
Use an empty alt attribute for decorative images (e.g. a glow behind a hero).
When using a builder's 'Copy settings'/'Paste settings' to apply loading and dimension attributes across many images, note that alt text can be overwritten.
After pasting, re-add any alt text that was lost.
Recognize that alt text supports accessibility and the presenter observes it also nudges PageSpeed scores, so it's a low-cost addition during the same pass.
caveats: Keep decorative and meaningful images distinct — meaningful images need descriptive alt, decorative ones get empty alt.
Copy/paste behavior is tool-specific; verify in your builder.
